II.
PURPOSE AND OVERVIEW OF TESTIMONY 
What is the purpose of your Direct Testimony? 
11 
The purpose of our Direct Testimony is to present evidence and provide a 
12 
recommended range for the Company’s cost of equity (sometimes referred 
13 
to as the “Return on Equity” or “ROE” for rate-setting purposes) and capital 
14 
structure for Corning Gas, the utility operating subsidiary of Holding 
15 
Company, as a stand-alone entity.  The ROE recommendation that is 
16 
presented in our Direct Testimony meets the capital attraction standards 
17 
established in Hope and Bluefield for Corning Gas on a stand-alone basis. 
18 
As such, the proxy groups that are discussed in Section V of our Direct 
19 
Testimony are comparable to the risk profile of Corning Gas, the natural 
20 
gas distribution utility that operates in the State of New York, not the 
21 
Holding Company, the parent company. Our analysis and recommendations 
22 
13


--- Page 14 ---
Q•

are supported by the detailed data presented in Schedules 1 (AEB/CMW-1) 
1 
through 12 (AEB/CMW-12) of Exhibit CNG-12.  
2 
3 
Please provide a brief overview of the analyses that led to your ROE 
4 
recommendation. 
5 
As discussed in more detail in the remainder of our Direct Testimony, it is 
6 
important to consider the results of several analytical approaches in 
7 
determining a reasonable recommendation for the Company’s ROE.  To 
8 
develop our ROE recommendation, we developed two proxy groups – the 
9 
Combined Utility Proxy Group and the Natural Gas Utility Proxy Group – 
10 
that consist of companies that face risk generally comparable to that faced 
11 
by the Company. The Combined Utility Proxy Group includes both electric 
12 
utilities and natural gas distribution utilities.  Recognizing that the ROE that 
13 
is being established in these proceedings is for natural gas distribution 
14 
companies, the Natural Gas Utility Proxy Group consists entirely of natural 
15 
gas distribution companies.  We developed a multi-stage Discounted Cash 
16 
Flow (“DCF”) model and two forms of the Capital Asset Pricing Model 
17 
(“CAPM”).  We have presented the DCF and CAPM results weighted 
18 
equally, and with the Commission’s conventional 2/3 weighting of the DCF 
19 
and 1/3 weighting of the CAPM.  We have considered the range of results 
20 
established using both the Natural Gas Proxy Group and the Combined 
21 
Utility Proxy Group because the Natural Gas Proxy Group, although limited 
22 
in size, is more risk comparable to the Company than the Combined Utility 
23 
Proxy Group.  
24

20 
III.
REGULATORY GUIDELINES AND FINANCIAL 
CONSIDERATIONS 
Please describe the guiding principles to be used in establishing the cost 
21 
of capital for a regulated utility. 
22 
The United States Supreme Court’s precedent-setting Hope and Bluefield
23 
cases established the standards for determining the reasonableness of a 
24 
utility’s allowed ROE.  Among the standards established by the Court in 
25 
those cases are:  (1) consistency with the returns on equity investments in 
26 
18


--- Page 19 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 9 of 118 
other businesses having similar or comparable risks; (2) adequacy of the 
1 
return to support credit quality and access to capital; and (3) an 
2 
understanding that the means of arriving at a fair return are not controlling, 
3 
only that the end result leads to just and reasonable rates.3
4 
5 
Based on those standards, the Commission’s order in these cases should 
6 
provide the Company with the opportunity to earn a ROE that is: (1) 
7 
adequate to attract capital at reasonable terms, thereby enabling them to 
8 
continue to provide safe, reliable service; (2) sufficient to support the 
9

1 
Please provide a brief summary of the purpose of the GFP. 
2 
The GFP was initiated because the Commission recognized that the DCF 
3 
method was particularly sensitive to interest rate fluctuations and was 
4 
producing returns far below those of other methodologies.5  The 
5 
Commission’s goal in opening the GFP was to reduce controversy around 
6 
ROE calculations and to attempt to find common ground on contentious 
7 
issues by developing a consensus approach for setting utility equity returns. 
8 
9 
The Commission examined whether there should be greater consistency in 
10 
rate of return determinations from company to company, such that 
11 
differences in authorized returns could be directly attributed to differences 
12 
in risk between companies.  In addition, the Commission examined whether 
13 
its historical primary reliance on the DCF method continued to provide fair 
14 
returns.6  The Commission’s inquiry considered the merits of a generic 
15 
process to reduce redundancy in litigating equity returns, and sought a 
16 
robust, but standardized, approach to setting ROE such that allowed returns 
17 
would be commensurate with the risk of the individual company and would 
18 
not be skewed by the shortcomings of a single methodology.

Is flexibility of approach and judgment important to ROE 
15 
determination? 
16 
Yes, it is.  When faced with the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts 
17 
are inclined to gather and evaluate as much relevant data (both quantitative 
18 
and qualitative) as can be reasonably analyzed.  Analysts and academics 
19 
understand that ROE models are tools to be used in the ROE estimation 
20 
process, and that strict adherence to any single approach, or the specific 
21 
results of any single approach, can lead to flawed conclusions.  No model 
22 
can exactly pinpoint the correct return on equity; rather, each model brings 
23 
its own perspective and set of inputs that inform the estimate of ROE.  That 
24 
26


--- Page 27 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 17 of 118 
position is consistent with the Hope finding that “[u]nder the statutory 
1 
standard of ‘just and reasonable,’ it is the result reached, not the method 
2 
employed, which is controlling.”11 
3 
4 
Though each model brings a different perspective and adds depth to the 
5 
analysis, each model also has its own set of inherent weaknesses and should 
6 
not be relied upon individually without corroboration from other 
7 
approaches.  Changes to inputs as a result of changes in economic 
8 
conditions could have widely different effects on the results of the various 
9 
analyses.   
10 
11 
Regardless of which analyses are performed to estimate the investor’s 
12 
required return on equity, the analyst must apply judgment to assess the 
13 
reasonableness of results and to determine the best weighting to apply to 
14 
results under prevailing capital market conditions.  No one model can 
15 
reliably and consistently estimate the cost of capital that meets the fairness 
16 
standard of Hope and Bluefield in all market conditions.

CAPITAL MARKET CONDITIONS 
Why is it important to analyze capital market conditions? 
19 
The ROE estimation models rely on market data that are specific to the 
20 
proxy group, in the case of the DCF model, or the market risk premium, in 
21 
11
Hope, 320 U.S., at 602.

--- Page 28 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 18 of 118 
the case of the CAPM.  The results of ROE estimation models can be 
1 
affected by prevailing market conditions at the time the analysis is 
2 
performed.  While the ROE that is established in a rate proceeding is 
3 
intended to be forward-looking, the practitioner uses current and projected 
4 
market data, specifically stock prices, dividends, growth rates, and interest 
5 
rates in the ROE estimation models to estimate the required return for the 
6 
subject company.   
7 
8 
Analysts and regulatory commissions recognize that current market 
9 
conditions affect the results of the ROE estimation models.  Accordingly, it 
10 
is important to consider the effect of these conditions on the ROE estimation 
11 
models when determining the appropriate range and recommended ROE for 
12 
a future period.  If investors do not expect current market conditions to be 
13 
sustained in the future, the ROE estimation may not provide an accurate 
14 
estimate of investors’ required return during that rate period.  Therefore, it 
15 
is very important to consider projected market data to estimate the return 
16 
for that forward-looking period.

1 
What effect, if any, will the Federal Reserve’s accommodative 
2 
monetary policy have on long-term interest rates over the near-term? 
3 
The Federal Reserve has acknowledged that they will keep the federal funds 
4 
rate near zero for the near-term.  The goal of the accommodative monetary 
5 
policy is to achieve the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate of maximum 
6 
employment and stable prices.  However, while the current accommodative 
7 
monetary policy will keep short-term interest rates low, it does not have a 
8 
direct effect on long-term interest rates.  Long-term interest rates can 
9 
increase even though monetary policy is accommodative.  In fact, one of 
10 
the leading indicators used by investors to determine what stage of the 
11 
business cycle the economy is in is to review the yield curve which shows 
12 
the difference between long-term and short-term interest rates. A flat or 
13 
inverted yield curve is when long-term interest rates are equivalent to or less 
14 
than short-term interest rates and usually occurs prior to a recession. 
15 
Conversely, a steepening yield curve is when the difference between long-
16 
term interest rates and short-term interest rates is increasing and indicates 
17 
that the economy is entering a period of economic expansion and inflation 
18 
following a recession.21

What is the effect of high valuations of utility stocks on the DCF model? 
1 
High valuations have the effect of depressing dividend yields, which results 
2 
in overall lower estimates of the cost of equity resulting from the DCF 
3 
model. The relatively low dividend yields demonstrated over the longer 
4 
historical period imply that the ROE calculated using historical market data 
5 
in the DCF model may understate the forward-looking cost of equity.  
6 
Therefore, the DCF model results must be interpreted with extreme caution 
7 
so as to not understate the cost of equity during the period that Corning Gas’ 
8 
rates will be in effect.

C. CONCLUSION
4 
What are your conclusions regarding the effect of current market 
5 
conditions on the cost of equity for Corning Gas? 
6 
Given the uncertainty and volatility that has characterized capital markets 
7 
in 2020 and 2021, it is reasonable that equity investors would now require 
8 
a higher return on equity to compensate them for the additional risk 
9 
associated with owning common stock under these market conditions.  
10 
Further, while the Federal Reserve will keep short-term interest rates low 
11 
over the next few years to support the economic recovery this does not 
12 
indicate that long-term interest rates cannot increase.  In fact, many equity 
13 
analysts believe long-term interest rates will increase in 2021 as the 
14 
economy enters the early expansion phase of the business cycle. 
15 
Historically, the utility sector has underperformed the broader market as 
16 
interest rates increase and the economy recovers. 
17 
18 
Investors’ current expectations regarding the economy highlights the 
19 
importance of using forward-looking inputs in the models used to estimate 
20 
the cost of equity.  While the share prices of utilities declined in response to 
21 
the economic effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, current utility valuations 
22 
are still well above the long-term average.  The current high valuations 
23 
result in low dividend yields for utilities, which means that DCF models 
24 
46


--- Page 47 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 37 of 118 
using recent historical data likely underestimate investors’ required return 
1 
for Corning Gas over the period that rates will be in effect.  This 
2 
consideration regarding the DCF model is important especially in light of 
3 
the expectation that the utility sector will underperform relative to the 
4 
broader market as the economy recovers from the COVID-19 pandemic. 
5 
Conversely, two out of three inputs (i.e., risk-free rate and market risk 
6 
premium) in the CAPM can be estimated using forward-looking 
7 
projections.  Therefore, the CAPM is likely to capture more effectively the 
8 
economic conditions expected by investors over the near-term.  This 
9 
highlights the importance of considering the results of each of the models 
10 
to reflect investors’ expectations of market conditions over the period that 
11 
the rates established in this proceeding will be in effect. 
12 
13 
Finally, credit rating agencies have demonstrated concerns about the cash 
14 
flow metrics of utilities related to the negative effects of both current market 
15 
conditions and the TCJA on utilities’ risk profile.  Therefore, it is 
16 
increasingly important to establish a rate of return and capital structure that 
17 
supports the Company’s cash flow metrics to enable Corning Gas the ability 
18 
to attract capital at reasonable terms during the period that rates will be in 
19 
effect.

V.
PROXY GROUP SELECTION 
Please explain why have you used a group of proxy companies to 
1 
estimate the cost of equity for the Company? 
2 
In this proceeding, we are estimating the cost of equity for a company that 
3 
has rate-regulated, natural gas distribution utility operations in New York.  
4 
Because ROE is a market-based concept and the Company is not publicly 
5 
traded, it is necessary to establish a group of companies that is both publicly 
6 
traded and comparable to Corning Gas in certain fundamental business and 
7 
financial respects to serve as proxies in the ROE estimation process.  The 
8 
proxy companies used in our analyses all possess a set of operating and risk 
9 
characteristics that are substantially comparable to the Company and thus 
10 
provide a reasonable basis for the derivation and assessment of the 
11 
Company’s ROE. 
12 
13 
In utility rate proceedings before the Commission over the past 25 years 
14 
(since the RD in the GFP),43 the Commission has endorsed the use of proxy 
15 
groups for the purpose of determining utility ROEs.  Because proxy 
16 
companies are now commonly used as the basis for estimating the utility 
17 
cost of equity, the primary objective of the screening process is to establish 
18 
a group of companies that is as comparable as possible to the subject 
19 
company with respect to fundamental financial and business risks.  While 
20 
the determination of an appropriate ROE necessarily requires a degree of 
21 
43
Generic Finance RD, at 133-134.

1 
VI.
COST OF EQUITY ESTIMATION 
Please briefly discuss the ROE in the context of the regulated Rate of 
2 
Return. 
3 
The rate of return (“ROR”) for a regulated utility is based on its weighted 
4 
average cost of capital, in which the costs of the individual sources of capital 
5 
are weighted by their respective percentages of total capitalization of the 
6 
utility.  The ROE included in the ROR is weighted by the percentage of 
7 
common equity in the regulated utility’s ratemaking capital structure. 
8 
9 
How is the required ROE determined? 
10 
While the cost of debt can be directly observed, the cost of equity and the 
11 
required ROE are market-based and, therefore, must be estimated based on 
12 
observable market information.  The required ROE is determined by using 
13 
one or more analytical techniques that rely on market data to quantify 
14 
investor expectations regarding the range of required equity returns.  
15 
Informed judgment is applied, based on the results of those analyses, to 
16 
determine where within the range of results the cost of equity for a company 
17 
falls.  As a general proposition, the key consideration in determining the 
18 
cost of equity is to ensure that the methodologies employed reasonably 
19 
reflect investors’ views of the financial markets, the proxy group 
20 
companies, and the subject company’s risk profile. 
21 
22 
61


--- Page 62 ---
Q• 
A. 
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 52 of 118 
What methods did you use to determine the Company’s cost of equity?  
1 
Consistent with Commission precedent, we used the DCF model and 
2 
CAPM as the primary approaches.  In establishing our recommended ROE, 
3 
we relied on a multi-stage form of the DCF model, and, consistent with the 
4 
Commission’s stated preference, we used both the traditional form of the 
5 
CAPM, as well as the Zero-Beta form of that model.  In both forms of the 
6 
CAPM, we incorporated a forward-looking measure of the Market Risk 
7 
Premium.  
8 
9 
Why do you believe it is important to use more than one analytical 
10 
approach? 
11 
Because the cost of equity is not directly observable, it must be estimated 
12 
based on both quantitative and qualitative information.  When faced with 
13 
the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts and investors are inclined 
14 
to gather and evaluate as much relevant data as reasonably can be 
15 
analyzed.  As a result, a number of models have been developed to estimate 
16 
the cost of equity.  For that reason, we use multiple approaches to estimate 
17 
the cost of equity.  As a practical matter, however, all of the models 
18 
available for estimating the cost of equity are subject to limiting 
19 
assumptions or other methodological constraints.  Consequently, many 
20 
finance texts recommend using multiple approaches when estimating the 
21 
cost of equity.  For example, Copeland, Koller, and Murrin57 suggest using 
22 
57
Tom Copeland, Tim Koller and Jack Murrin, Valuation: Measuring and Managing the 
Value of Companies, 3rd Ed. (New York: McKinsey & Company, Inc., 2000), at 214.

1 
Gapenski58 recommend the CAPM, DCF, and “bond yield plus risk 
2 
premium” approaches.59  
3 
4 
How are current market conditions affecting the results of the DCF and 
5 
CAPM models?  
6 
As discussed in Section IV, the results of the DCF model are understating 
7 
the forward-looking cost of equity.  The CAPM method offers some balance 
8 
to the sensitivity of the DCF model to low Treasury bond yields.  However, 
9 
low interest rates also impact the CAPM in two ways: (1) if the risk-free 
10 
rate is based on historical average yields on Treasury bonds, it understates 
11 
the forward-looking risk-free rate, and (2) if the market risk premium is 
12 
based on historical returns on large company stocks minus the historical 
13 
average risk-free rate, it understates the forward-looking market risk 
14 
premium.  To adjust for these shortcomings, the risk-free rate in the CAPM 
15 
analysis should also consider projected yields on Treasury bonds, and the 
16 
market risk premium should be based on a forward-looking computation of 
17 
the expected return on the total market less the risk-free rate.  Market risk 
18 
premiums based on long-term historical averages are unresponsive to 
19

A. DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW MODEL
4 
Please describe the DCF approach. 
5 
The DCF approach is based on the theory that a stock’s current market price 
6 
represents the present value of all expected future cash flows.  In its most 
7 
general form, the DCF model is expressed as follows in Equation [1]: 
8 
𝑃0 =
𝐷1
(1+𝑟)1 +
𝐷2
(1+𝑟)2 + ⋯+
𝐷𝑛
(1+𝑟)𝑛
[1]
9 
Where P0 represents the current market stock price, D1 … Dn are all 
10 
expected future dividends, and r is the discount rate, or required ROE.  As 
11 
discussed below, we have not included the constant growth form of the DCF 
12 
model, but instead have focused on a multi-stage form of the DCF model.   
13 
14 
Please generally describe the DCF model you relied on.  
15 
The multi-stage DCF model is an extension of the constant growth form that 
16 
enables the analyst to specify growth rates over multiple stages.  As with 
17 
the constant growth form of the DCF model, the multi-stage form defines 
18 
the cost of equity as the discount rate that sets the current price equal to the 
19 
discounted value of future cash flows.  A multi-stage DCF model addresses 
20 
the possibility that mean five-year growth rates may not be reasonable in 
21 
perpetuity and that payout ratios could vary over time. 
22 
23 
65


--- Page 66 ---
Q• 
A. 
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 56 of 118 
Please describe the structure of the multi-stage DCF model.  
1 
The multi-stage DCF model that we have used sets the proxy company’s 
2 
current stock price equal to the present value of future cash flows received 
3 
over three time periods.  In all three periods, cash flows are equal to the 
4 
annual dividend payments that stockholders receive.  The first period is a 
5 
short-term growth period that consists of the first five years; the second 
6 
period is a transition period from the short-term growth rate to the long-term 
7 
growth rate that occurs over five years (i.e., years 6 through 10); and the 
8 
third period is a long-term growth period that begins in year 11 and 
9 
continues in perpetuity.  The ROE is then calculated as the rate of return 
10 
that results from the initial stock investment and the dividend payments over 
11 
the analytical period. 
12 
13 
Has the Commission relied on a multi-stage DCF model in prior cases?  
14 
Yes, the Commission has relied on a two-stage form of the DCF model in 
15 
prior cases.60  The two-stage model that the Commission has relied on and 
16 
the multi-stage model that we rely on both define the cost of equity as the 
17 
discount rate that sets the current stock price equal to the discounted value 
18 
of future cash flows that are expressed as projected dividends.  Both models 
19 
project dividends using growth rates over multiple periods.   
20 
21 
60
See Case 10-E-0362, Proceeding on Motion of the Commission as to the Rates, Charges, 
Rules and Regulations of Orange and Rockland Utilities, Inc. for Electric Service, Order 
Establishing Rates for Electric Service, (issued June 17, 2011) (“2011 O&R Rate Order”), 
at 68-69.

3

6

8

Does the multi-stage form of the DCF model offer improvements over

Page 59 of 118 
Why do you believe that earnings growth rates are the appropriate 
1 
growth rates in the DCF model? 
2 
Earnings are the fundamental driver of a company’s ability to pay 
3 
dividends; therefore, earnings growth is the appropriate measure of a 
4 
company’s long-term growth. As noted by Brigham and Houston: 
5 
Growth in dividends occurs primarily as a result of 
6 
growth in earnings per share (EPS).  Earnings growth, 
7 
in turn, results from a number of factors, including (1) 
8 
inflation, (2) the amount of earnings the company 
9 
retains and invests, and (3) the rate of return the 
10 
company earns on its equity (ROE).62
11 
12 
In contrast, changes in a company’s dividend payments are based on 
13 
management decisions related to cash management and other factors.  For 
14 
example, a company may decide to retain certain earnings rather than 
15 
include those earnings in a dividend issuance.  Therefore, dividend growth 
16 
rates are less likely than earnings growth rates to reflect investor perceptions 
17 
of a company’s growth prospects.   
18 
19 
Is there support for the use of analysts’ earnings growth estimates in 
20 
the DCF model? 
21 
Yes, there is significant academic support for the use of analysts’ earnings 
22 
growth rates.  In addition, the majority of the data that are publicly available 
23 
to investors sets forth analysts’ projections of earnings growth rates.  Value 
24

Why is the long-term GDP growth rate a reasonable estimate of long-
1 
term growth in the multi-stage DCF model? 
2 
Long-term estimates of GDP growth are commonly used in regulatory 
3 
proceedings as a proxy for the long-term growth rate in the multi-stage DCF 
4 
analysis.  That application is based on the common theoretical assumption 
5 
that, over the long-run, all companies in the economy will tend to grow at 
6 
the same constant rate.  That assumption is designed to address the 
7 
uncertainty associated with estimating individual company growth rates 
8 
over very long-time horizons and is not meant to suggest that company 
9 
growth rates in the economy will indeed converge in practice over any given 
10 
period.   
11 
12 
Is your calculation of GDP growth consistent with the way in which 
13 
other analysts compute estimates of long-term GDP growth? 
14 
Yes.  Investors understand that the U.S. economy goes through cycles of 
15 
growth and contraction.  Therefore, it is appropriate to consider the longest 
16 
period possible to measure historical real growth in GDP.  This view is 
17 
consistent with Morningstar’s explanation about measuring GDP growth: 
18 
Growth in real GDP (with only a few exceptions) has 
19 
been reasonably stable over time; therefore, its 
20 
historical performance is a good estimate of expected 
21 
long-term future performance.  By combining the 
22 
inflation estimate with the real growth rate estimate, a 
23 
long-term estimate of nominal growth is formed.81
24 
25 
81
Ibbotson and Associates, Stocks, Bonds, Bills and Inflation, 1926-2012, 2013 Valuation

B. CAPITAL ASSET PRICING MODEL 
12 
Please briefly describe the Capital Asset Pricing Model. 
13 
The CAPM is a risk premium approach that estimates the market cost of 
14 
equity for a given security as a function of a risk-free return plus a risk 
15 
premium (to compensate investors for the non-diversifiable or “systematic” 
16 
risk of that security).  As shown in Equation [2], the CAPM is defined by 
17 
four components: 
18 
ke = rf + β(rm – rf)  
 [2]

Did you consider another form of the CAPM in your analysis? 
1 
Yes.  In prior proceedings, the Commission has relied upon the Zero-Beta 
2 
CAPM (the form of which is sometimes referred to as the “Empirical 
3 
CAPM”91) in estimating the cost of equity.  The Zero-Beta CAPM 
4 
calculates the product of the adjusted Beta coefficient and the market risk 
5 
premium and applies a weight of 75.00 percent to that result.  The model 
6 
then applies a 25.00 percent weight to the market risk premium, without any 
7 
effect from the Beta coefficient.  The results of the two calculations are 
8 
summed, along with the risk-free rate, to produce the Zero-Beta CAPM 
9 
result, as noted in Equation [4] below:   
10 
ke = rf + 0.75β(rm – rf) + 0.25(rm – rf)  
[4] 
11 
where: 
12 
ke = the required market ROE 
13 
β = Adjusted Beta coefficient of an individual security 
14 
rf = the risk-free rate of return 
15 
rm = the required return on the market as a whole 
16 
17 
In essence, the Zero-Beta form of the CAPM addresses the tendency of the 
18 
“traditional” CAPM to underestimate the cost of equity for companies with 
19 
low Beta coefficients such as regulated utilities.  In that regard, the Zero-
20 
Beta CAPM is not redundant to the use of adjusted Betas; rather, it 
21 
recognizes the results of academic research indicating that the risk-return 
22

term.92

Are the assumptions used in the CAPM less reliable than the 
11

12 
Not necessarily.  As discussed previously, the CAPM relies on a risk-free

14

15

18

20

21

VII. REGULATORY AND BUSINESS RISKS 
A. REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT
3 
Please explain how the regulatory framework affects investors’ risk 
4 
assessments. 
5 
The ratemaking process is premised on the principle that, for investors and 
6 
companies to commit the capital needed to provide safe and reliable utility 
7 
services, the subject utility must have the opportunity to recover invested 
8 
capital and the market-required return on such capital.  Regulatory 
9 
commissions recognize that because utility operations are capital intensive, 
10 
regulatory decisions should enable the utility to attract capital at reasonable 
11 
terms, which balance the long-term interests of investors and customers.  In 
12 
that respect, the regulatory framework in which a utility operates is one of 
13 
the most important factors considered in both debt and equity investors’ risk 
14 
assessments.  
15 
16 
Because investors have many investment alternatives, even within a given 
17 
market sector, the Company’s authorized return must be adequate on a 
18 
relative basis to ensure its ability to attract capital under a variety of 
19 
economic and financial market conditions.  From the perspective of debt 
20 
investors, the authorized return should enable the Company to generate the 
21 
cash flow needed to meet their near-term financial obligations, make the 
22 
92


--- Page 93 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 83 of 118 
capital investments needed to maintain and expand their systems, and 
1 
maintain sufficient levels of liquidity to fund unexpected events.  This 
2 
financial liquidity must be derived not only from internally-generated funds, 
3 
but also from efficient access to capital markets.     
4 
5 
From the perspective of equity investors, the authorized return must be 
6 
adequate to provide a risk-comparable return on the equity portion of the 
7 
Company’s capital investments.  Because equity investors are the residual 
8 
claimants on the Company’s cash flows (that is, debt interest must be paid 
9 
prior to any equity dividends), equity investors are particularly concerned 
10 
with the regulatory framework in which a utility operates and its effect on 
11 
future earnings and cash flows. 
12 
13

17 
credit ratings based on four key factors:

D. SMALL SIZE RISK
1 
Please explain the risk associated with small size. 
2 
Both the financial and academic communities have long accepted the 
3 
proposition that the Cost of Equity for small firms is subject to a “size 
4 
effect”.  While empirical evidence of the size effect often is based on studies 
5 
of industries other than regulated utilities, utility analysts also have noted 
6 
the risk associated with small market capitalizations.  Specifically, an 
7 
analyst for Ibbotson Associates noted: 
8 
For small utilities, investors face additional obstacles, 
9 
such as a smaller customer base, limited financial 
10 
resources, and a lack of diversification across 
11 
customers, energy sources, and geography.  These 
12 
obstacles imply a higher investor return.119
13 
14 
How does the smaller size of a utility affect its business risk? 
15 
In general, smaller companies are less able to withstand adverse events that 
16 
affect their revenues and expenses.  The impact of weather variability, the 
17 
loss of large customers to bypass opportunities, or the destruction of 
18 
demand as a result of general macroeconomic conditions or fuel price 
19 
volatility will have a proportionately greater impact on the earnings and 
20 
cash flow volatility of smaller utilities.  Similarly, capital expenditures for 
21 
non-revenue producing investments, such as system maintenance and 
22 
replacements, will put proportionately greater pressure on customer costs, 
23 
potentially leading to customer attrition or demand reduction.  Taken 
24 
119
Michael Annin, Equity and the Small-Stock Effect, Public Utilities Fortnightly, October 
15, 1995. 
112

A. 
Q•

together, these risks affect the return required by investors for smaller 
1 
companies.

17

IX.
MULTI-YEAR RATE PLAN 
Is the Company proposing a multi-year rate plan? 
1 
Yes. The Company is proposing a three-year rate plan ending in June 30, 
2 
2025.  
3 
4 
Would a multi-year rate plan impact your ROE recommendation?   
5 
Yes, it would.  The Commission has in many cases approved three-year rate 
6 
case settlements that often include stay-out premiums.  It is our 
7 
understanding that the Company will provide three years of forecast data in 
8 
their rate filings.  In keeping with Commission precedent, a stay-out 
9 
premium would reflect the increased risk faced by the Company under a 
10 
multi-year rate plan. 
11 
12 
How has New York typically estimated a stay-out premium?  
13 
The New York approach has typically set the measure of the risk and return 
14 
trade-off using one half of the yield spread between a one-year and three-
15 
year Treasury securities.   
16 
17 
Does one half of the yield spread between one-year and three-year 
18 
Treasuries sufficiently reflect the risk to equity investors inherent in a 
19 
multi-year stay-out?  
20 
No.  The stay-out premium associated with a multi-year rate plan should not 
21 
only compensate investors for changes in the level of interest rates or 
22 
124


--- Page 125 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 115 of 118 
inflation, but also for the potential risk of under-earning that is introduced 
1 
by “staying out.”  By staying out of rate cases, the utility may not fully 
2 
recover material amounts of capital expenditures and may be required to 
3 
absorb losses due to differences between the cost of service established in 
4 
the rate plan and actual levels of revenue and expense.  The premium should 
5 
compensate the utility and its investors for these additional risks over and 
6 
above interest rate risk.   
7 
8 
Have current market conditions increased the risk of a multi-year stay-
9 
out for the Company? 
10 
Yes. As noted earlier in my testimony, the economy is currently entering 
11 
the expansion phase of the business cycle.  Thus, investors expect economic 
12 
growth and inflation to increase in the near-term which will result in 
13 
increases in long-term interest rates.  Investors will rotate out of long-term 
14 
government bonds to avoid being locked into to low interest rates for the 
15 
long-term.  As a result, in the current market environment, there is 
16 
additional risk that the authorized ROE for the latter years of a multi-year 
17 
rate plan will be lower than investors’ future requirements as interest rates 
18 
are expected to increase.

realities of the business, particularly the need for capital expenditures, require 
continuous borrowing. Although Corning LDC has a good relationship with its

terminations and uncollectible accounts. Also in relation to capital expenditures, the 
2017 Rate Order includes requirements for the justification of capital expenditures, as 
well as unit-cost tracking of capital expenditures.

VIII. CONCLUSION 
Q. 
Please summarize the Panel's conclusions regarding whether the proposed Transaction 
should be found to be in the public interest. 
A. 
Our testimony, together with that of the Argo Panel, demonstrates that the proposed 
acquisition of Corning LDC by ACP Crotona is in the public interest because it will 
produce positive benefits for Corning LDC's customers and the communities Corning 
LDC serves. In addition to the more detailed discussion by the Argo Panel of how the 
public interest standard of PSL §70 is met, we would like to emphasize three points 
that should weigh heavily in favor of the Transaction. First and foremost, the 
Transaction will provide Corning LDC with the much-needed access to capital on 
reasonable terms that is critical to Corning LDC's ability to provide safe and reliable 
service to its customers. Second, by recognizing Corning LDC's strength as a small, 
well-run utility and committing to maintaining the existing workforce and 
management, the Transaction will take advantage of those resources by providing 
Corning LDC management with the autonomy it requires to address its unique local 
circumstances and to assure continuity in operations. Third, the Transaction has no 
risk to Corning LDC's customers or the communities in which Corning LDC operates. 
As we have discussed in this testimony, Corning LDC and its customers need

VII. 
STANDARD FOR APPROVAL OF ACQUISITION 
10 
A. 
The “Public Interest” Standard 
11 
Q. 
Are you familiar with the legal standard that governs the Commission’s consideration of 
12 
utility acquisitions in New York? 
13 
A. 
Argo is advised by counsel that, under PSL Section 70, approval of a Transaction of 
14 
this nature requires that the transaction be shown to be in the “public interest.”  It has 
15 
also been informed that the Commission, in assessing whether a Transaction is in the 
16 
“public interest,” requires that the transaction produce “positive net benefits,” and that, 
17 
to determine whether that is the case, the Commission considers (1) the expected 
18 
benefits attributable to the transaction, offset by (2) risks or detriments remaining after 
19 
(3) reasonable mitigation measures.  (This analysis is described in greater detail in the 
20 
Petition.)  It is further understood that, if the foregoing analysis results in a conclusion 
21 
that the risks remaining after mitigation are not outweighed by the benefits of the 
22 
transaction, the Commission may require that those benefits be supplemented by 
23 
monetized benefits commonly referred to as “positive benefit adjustments” or “PBAs.” 
24

15

 The purpose of my testimony is to address cost and revenue allocation.  In so doing, 
16 
I will address the Direct Testimony of Mr. Paul Normand, witness for CNG. 
17 
Q.  
DID YOU REVIEW THE EMBEDDED COST OF SERVICE STUDY 
18 
(“ECOSS”) PRESENTED BY THE COMPANY? 
19 
A. 
Yes.  The Company’s ECOSS and proposed revenue allocation was presented by Mr. 
20 
Normand in his Direct Testimony and Exhibits.  In general, an ECOSS is a traditional 
21 
study wherein revenue requirements are allocated among customer classes on the basis 
22 
of cost causation. 
23 
Q. 
WHY IS AN ECOSS IMPORTANT? 
24 
186


--- Page 187 ---
Case No. 21-G-0394 
 
Richard Baudino 
 
 
 
Page 3 
 
 
 
A. 
An ECOSS illustrates the costs a utility incurs to serve each customer class.  It is 
1 
widely accepted that costs should be allocated among customer classes on the basis of 
2 
cost causation.  That principle is generally applied to costs that cannot be directly 
3 
assigned to a particular customer class.  As such, costs should be allocated to those 
4 
classes on the basis of how or why those costs are incurred by the utility.  The results 
5 
of such studies are normally relied upon in assigning cost and revenue responsibilities 
6 
to various customer classes. 
7 
Q. 
DO YOU SUPPORT THE PREMISE THAT COST CAUSATION PRINCIPLES 
8 
SHOULD GUIDE THE ALLOCATION OF COSTS TO THE VARIOUS 
9 
CUSTOMER CLASSES? 
10 
A. 
Yes.  Rates that are based on consistently applied cost causation principles are fair and 
11 
reasonable and further the causes of stability, conservation and economic efficiency.  
12 
Other factors such as simplicity, gradualism, economic development and ease of 
13 
administration may also be taken into consideration when determining the final 
14 
allocation of the revenue requirement among classes.  In addition, changes in ECOSS 
15 
methodology yielding disparate results, such as here, may cause parties to reconsider  
16 
overreliance on particular ECOSS results. 
17 
Q. 
PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE AND DEVELOPMENT OF A CLASS 
18 
COST OF SERVICE STUDY. 
19 
A 
A class cost of service study allocates and assigns the total cost of providing utility 
20 
service to the classes of customers receiving that service.  The development of a class 
21 
cost of service study consists of three steps: functionalization, classification, and 
22 
allocation.  Functionalization refers to the process by which the Company’s 
23 
investments and expenses are identified and segregated into different cost categories.  
24 
187


--- Page 188 ---
Case No. 21-G-0394 
 
Richard Baudino 
 
 
 
Page 4 
 
 
 
For CNG, these functional categories include transmission, distribution, metering and 
1 
billing, and various customer accounts and service expenses.     
2 
 
 
Once functionalization is complete, the utility’s costs are classified into 
3 
categories of demand-related, energy related and customer-related costs in order to 
4 
facilitate the allocation of costs by applying cost causation principles.  In general, all 
5 
distribution costs are either responsive to increases in natural gas demand or to the 
6 
number of customers.  Demand-related costs are those that are needed to serve the 
7 
winter peak demands of distribution customers.  Demand-related costs are fixed and 
8 
do not vary with the monthly and annual commodity consumption of the utility’s 
9 
customers.  Customer-related costs are associated with the number of customers and 
10 
are costs that are incurred to connect customers to the system independent of the 
11 
customer’s demand and energy requirements.  Primary examples of customer-related 
12 
costs are investments in meters, services, and a portion of main investment incurred to 
13 
extend the distribution system to the customer’s premises and conform to local and 
14 
national codes and standards.  In addition, such accounting functions as meter reading, 
15 
bill preparation and revenue accounting are generally considered customer-related 
16 
costs. 
17 
 
 
Lastly, the functionalized and classified costs are allocated to the various 
18 
customer classes based on each class’ contribution to the respective cost 
19 
classifications.  In general, demand-related costs are allocated based on each class’ 
20 
contribution to the maximum demand placed on the system by the classes or by the 
21 
customers within the classes.  Customer-related costs are allocated based upon the 
22 
number of customers in each class, weighted to account for the complexity of servicing 
23 
the needs of the different classes of customers.

5

6

7 
example, if a customer class rate of return is 5.5% and the system average rate of return 
8 
is 6.5%, then that class RROR is 0.85 (5.5% divided by 6.5%). Because the 0.85 
9 
RROR is below 1.0, the class is earning less than the system average rate of return.  A 
10 
class RROR of 1.0 indicates that the class return is the same as the system average rate 
11 
of return.  A class RROR greater than 1.0 indicates that the class RROR is greater than 
12 
the system average rate of return.  The “2020 CNG ECOSS” columns present class 
13 
returns and RRORs from Case No. 20-G-0101.  The “2021 CNG ECOSS” columns 
14

into compliance with cathodic protection requirement towards the 10.0-mile target.”

Without the elimination of duplicate bare steel, abandonment of LPP in areas where gas 
2

3 
would have been short of our LPP target the last three years.  There are ample and sound

18

7

8

9 
meant to give management flexibility to accommodate changing operational 
10

11 
may determine to forgo expenditures on items such as the Roof or Parking Lot repairs 
12

13 
as pipe replacement or storm restoration projects.

2 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (“CLCPA”) 
3 
Q. 
What is the CLCPA and how does it affect the Company? 
4 
A. 
The CLCPA is New York State legislation, enacted in 2019, that is designed to reduce 
5 
greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions over the next several years.  The CLCPA 
6 
mandates, among many other things, the reduction of GHG emissions to 60% of 1990 
7 
levels by the year 2030, and to 15% of 1990 levels by the year 2050, with the 
8 
remaining emission reduction achieved by controlled offsets.
9 
Q. 
Has the CLCPA policy issue been addressed in previous Corning rate cases? 
10 
A. 
Yes.  In Case 20-G-0101 the Company proposed to shorten depreciation lives of plant 
11 
assets to correspond with the statutory date of the required reduction of New York 
12 
GHG emissions to 15% of 1990 levels, which, in Case 20-G-0101, was 30 years. 
13 
Q. 
Why did Corning make such a proposal? 
14 
A. 
The CLCPA, in conjunction with additional legislation proposed by the Governor, is 
15 
intended to reduce and then eliminate GHG emissions in New York State.  Over a now 
16 
much shorter period of time, this legislation will reduce the number of natural gas 
17 
customers and the volume of natural gas use, thus reducing customer revenues and 
18 
revenues per customer.  The CLCPA will thereby put pressure on the Company’s 
19 
access to external capital, thus increasing costs to safely deliver natural gas to its 
20 
customers.  The CLCPA poses a double edged threat to the Company. While its 
21 
greenhouse gas emission mandates will undeniably reduce its customer base and 
22 
customer revenues, this legislation, and the Commission’s orders, require the 
23 
260


--- Page 261 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-7 
Company to continue to invest capital to improve the safety and reliability of the 
1 
Company’s infrastructure, as well as to reduce leaks and other emissions.  It is critical 
2 
that new mandated capital expenditures be financed primarily with internally 
3 
generated funds (principally depreciation) and that depreciable lives match the 
4 
expected economic lives of utility assets.  The Company believes that either 
5 
systematic replacement capital expenditures must be curtailed or the depreciable lives 
6 
of assets need to be shortened.  It is imperative that depreciable lives are reconciled 
7 
with the expectations of the CLCPA in this case, rather than delaying such action. 
8 
Further, gas mains that are mandated for abandonment should be depreciated over 
9 
their useful lives determined by reference to their scheduled abandonment.  Current 
10 
nominal gas commodity prices are relatively low, so consumer impacts will be 
11 
mitigated.  As I will explain later in this section, proposed federal legislation will most 
12 
likely significantly increase natural gas production costs, and these production cost 
13 
increases will be passed on to LDCs in the form of increased gas commodity prices, 
14 
and these future price increases will then be passed on to an ever shrinking gas 
15 
customer base.  For these reasons, it is important to stabilize/reduce rate base while the 
16 
Company’s customer count remains high.  Finally, it is a confiscatory policy to 
17 
mandate large capital expenditures in order to abandon leak prone pipe, even for 
18 
safety reasons, and not provide depreciable lives consistent with the abandonment of 
19 
leak prone pipe.  Realistic depreciation lives for gas mains scheduled for abandonment 
20 
will help accommodate the CLCPA timetable. 
21 
As the mandates of the CLCPA take effect, volumes will be reduced and rate base 
22 
should decline in parallel.

Productivity Imputation and Inflation Allowance 
13 
Q. 
Can you provide historical perspective on the Commission’s application of the 
14 
productivity imputation? 
15 
A. 
Yes.  In the recent past, a productivity adjustment of at least 1% has been applied 
16 
virtually automatically in rate cases in New York.  Indeed, in the 2009 Rate Order in 
17 
Case 08-G-1137, the Commission adopted a productivity adjustment of 2%.  In the 
18 
April 20, 2012 Order Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal and Establishing a Multi-Year 
19 
Rate Plan (the “2012 Rate Order”) in Case 11-G-0280, the Commission adopted an 
20 
adjustment of 1%.  Originally, the Commission would apply such an adjustment in the 
21 
absence of a clear demonstration that there was at least 1% productivity already 
22 
included in the historical test year that would continue through the rate year. 
23 
279


--- Page 280 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-26 
Q. 
Do you believe that the 1% or 2 % productivity adjustment is warranted in this case? 
1 
A. 
No.  The Commission’s October 18, 2007 Order in an Orange and Rockland Utilities, 
2 
Inc. rate proceeding (Cases 06-E-1433, 06-E-1547), stated that the productivity 
3 
adjustment “is a surrogate for specific adjustments to overall productivity gains” 
4 
(p. 19).  If productivity is achieved by a utility, there is no justification for applying 
5 
the “surrogate.”  Corning has clearly increased its productivity by reducing costs, as 
6 
discussed below.  Such control and avoidance of costs demonstrates that at least the 
7 
equivalent of a 2% productivity adjustment is already embedded in customer rates and, 
8 
therefore, no further productivity adjustment is necessary or appropriate. 
9 
Q. 
Can you describe Corning’s productivity achievements? 
10 
A.
Yes.  First and foremost, Corning has developed and expanded the business of 
11 
transporting locally produced natural gas from the wellhead into the Company’s 
12 
system and into interstate pipeline systems.  Since 2010, the amount of revenues 
13 
derived from this effort has resulted in revenue pass back to customers of 
14 
approximately $6.2 million.  In addition to their share of transportation revenues, 
15 
customers are benefitting from lower overall gas costs because locally produced gas 
16 
requires less transportation than traditional supplies from the Gulf Coast and other 
17 
distant sources.  Corning consistently has some of the lowest cost gas in the State.  
18 
Over both the near and the long term, therefore, Corning’s customers stand to benefit 
19 
substantially from the Company’s innovation and creativity. 
20 
As with construction of pipelines and compressor stations to transport locally 
21 
produced gas, such expansion of the system in new service territories is not something 
22 
Corning is required to do in order to meet its public service obligations; it is a 
23 
280


--- Page 281 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-27 
voluntary undertaking with both near and long-term benefits to Company customers, 
1 
both existing and new.  The Commission has encouraged infrastructure expansion to 
2 
lower customer fuel costs and promote economic activity.  Corning is at the forefront 
3 
of this activity.  Corning’s franchise in Virgil is an example of where this Company

15

15 
A. 
Yes.  Although the Commission typically addresses health insurance cost increases in 
16

17

18

19 
Q. 
Please explain. 
20 
A. 
The Commission’s practice is to include health insurance in the general inflation pool.  
21 
While this practice may have been justified in the distant past when health cost 
22 
increases were more closely aligned with other cost increases, those days are long 
23 
282


--- Page 283 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-29 
gone.  Unfortunately, health insurance costs continue to outpace inflation by a 
1 
substantial margin.  The Commission’s practice, and Staff’s adherence to it, has 
2 
unfortunately become a convenient “methodology” that guarantees that Corning and 
3 
other utilities will never recover the full cost of health insurance.  I recommend that 
4 
the Commission abandon this approach.  Objectively, it has become untenable and 
5 
warrants re-examination based on current circumstances.  It should be noted that 
6 
Corning goes out to bid for health insurance every year, has increased the premium 
7 
paid by employees and has taken other actions to limit the increase in health care 
8 
costs.  For example, included in the services provided by our group captive insurance 
9 
company, we now have available nurse triage services that will allow Company 
10 
employees to consult with a licensed nurse if an employee is injured or becomes ill at 
11 
work.  This service should result in reduced costs of employees seeking emergency 
12 
room health care when such care is not necessary. 
13 
Q. 
What conditions lead you to question the Commission’s typical treatment of health 
14 
care cost increases? 
15 
A. 
The dominant condition is the difference for Corning between the general inflation 
16 
rate and the medical inflation rate (a differential of 2.47X).  The cumulative general 
17 
inflation rate is 12.05%, while the cumulative medical inflation rate is projected to be 
18 
29.71% from the historical test period to the first Rate Year. 
19 
Q. 
Have you performed calculations specific to Corning on this issue? 
20 
A. 
Yes.  Exhibit CNG-9, Schedule 2, presents my analysis. 
21 
Q. 
What does the analysis show? 
22 
283


--- Page 284 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-30 
A. 
The analysis shows that, in order for Corning to recover its projected health care cost 
1 
it must experience significant cost decreases in all other items in the inflation pool.  
2 
This conclusion flows principally from (a) the fact that health care costs constitute a 
3 
significant proportion of the inflation pool (26% of the total); and (b) the rate 
4 
differential of 2.47X, as discussed above.  As a consequence, the other items included 
5 
in the general inflation allowance of $322,878 (i.e., excluding medical) would have to 
6 
decrease by $102,781, or 31% less than the projected amount, to offset the medical 
7 
cost increases. 
8 
Q. 
What do you conclude from the analysis presented in Exhibit CNG-9, Schedule 2? 
9 
A. 
The notion, assumed in the current Commission practice, that Corning’s health care 
10 
cost can be offset by “managing” the rest of the inflation pool expenses, i.e., by 
11 
bringing about cost decreases in other items in the general pool, is not sustainable.  
12 
The effect of continuing this myth is an imputation of additional “productivity” that 
13 
knows no rational basis and could be considered confiscatory by not providing for 
14 
recovery of legitimate operating costs. 
15 
Q.

16 
escalation of health insurance at the general inflation rate? 
17 
A. 
Yes.  If the Commission were to impute a productivity adjustment and allow health 
18 
insurance cost at the general inflation rate the effective productivity adjustment would 
19 
be 2.89 % (assuming 1% productivity) or 3.89% (assuming 2% productivity) of 
20 
controllable other O&M expense (see Exhibit CNG-9, Schedule 2). 
21

What do you recommend?

Q. 
Please describe the issue between Staff and the Company. 
13 
A. 
The Company’s calculation of the tax sur-credit for Rate Year 1 carries forward for 
14 
each of Rate Years 2 and 3.  The sur-credit for Rate Year 2 gets carried forward to 
15 
Rate Year 3.  The Company’s calculations result in a tax sur-credit for Rate Year 1 
16 
that equals the amount calculated for Rate Year 1 ($336,755).  The sur-credit for Rate 
17 
Year 2 equals the amount required for Rate Year 1 ($336,755), plus the amount 
18 
calculated for Rate Year 2 ($425,423), which equals $762,178.  For Rate Year 3, the 
19 
tax sur-credit equals the amount calculated for Rate Years 1 and 2 ($762,148), plus the 
20 
amount calculated for Rate Year 3 ($31,252), for a total sur-credit for Rate Year 3 of 
21 
$793,430.  The total tax sur-credit for the three Rate Years is $1,892,363.

1 
RateYear.  For Rate Years 2 and 3, Staff’s calculations produce differences from the 
2

3 
differ is in the application of the carry-forward from Rate Year 1 to Rate Year 2, and 
4

5

7

11

13

DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-44 
1 
Q. 
Why do you believe the Company’s calculation is correct? 
2 
A. 
A review of the Commission’s Tax Rate Order leads to the conclusion that the purpose 
3 
of this exercise is to determine how much revenue should be refunded to customers so 
4 
that customers would be made whole for the decrease in federal income tax rates.  To 
5 
achieve that objective, the utility company should refund to customers the amount of 
6 
revenues that would produce the exact same amount of after-tax earnings that the 
7 
utility would have realized had the utility’s revenue requirement been based on the 
8 
298


--- Page 299 ---
4818-6387-2497.5 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF CHARLES LENNS 
CL-45 
new federal income tax rate of 21%, as opposed to the pre-2018 federal income tax 
1 
rate of 34%.  The Company’s calculation produces this result as detailed in Exhibit 
2 
CNG-14, Summary, and Schedule 3, pages 1 to 3.  For Rate Years 1, 2 and 3, applying 
3 
the Company’s tax sur-credit methodology, the Company had after-tax earnings for 
4 
three years equal to $3,450,558, $3,657,251, and $3,838,615, respectively at the 34% 
5 
tax rate.  After applying the Company calculated sur-credit for each year, after-tax 
6 
earnings equal the exact same amounts of $3,450,558, $3,657,251, and $3,838,615, 
7 
respectively. 
8 
Applying staff’s methodology (Exhibit CNG-14, Schedule 4, pages 1 to 3), it can be 
9 
seen that after-tax earnings for the Company are lower after applying the tax sur-credit 
10 
than they are before the tax sur-credit. The after-tax earnings before the sur-credit at 
11 
34% are $3,450,558, $3,657,251, and $3,838,615, respectively.  After-tax earnings by 
12 
applying Staff’s sur-credit methodology, at a 21% tax rate, equal $3,450,558, 
13 
$3,423,568, and $3,040,254, respectively.  
14 
Staff’s method produces a result that puts the Company in a worse position at a 21% 
15 
tax rate after applying the tax sur-credit than the Company would be under a 34% tax 
16 
rate without a tax sur-credit.  This result could not have been intended by the 
17 
Commission’s order.  
18 
Q. 
What do you conclude from your analysis? 
19 
A. 
I conclude that the Company’s sur-credit amount of $1,892,363 is the amount that is 
20 
owed to customers per the Commission’s Tax Rate Order in Case 17-M-0815.

WEATHER NORMALIZATION 
16 
Q.   
What is the purpose of a weather normalization adjustment? 
17 
A.   
For the purposes of cost of service studies and rate making, the test year must represent 
18 
typical or normal circumstances.  The Company has identified specific pro forma 
19 
adjustments to the test year to reflect the expenses that normally would be anticipated in 
20 
the test year, based on those changes which are known and measurable at the present 
21 
time.  However, another important adjustment is the Company’s ccf sales which are 
22 
weather sensitive.  Even small variations in weather can have a material impact on the 
23 
366


--- Page 367 ---
MO( 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 6 of 21 
sales and related revenues, especially for a gas utility.  The weather normalization 
1 
adjustment is targeted to identify the change in sales and revenue that would have been 
2 
anticipated if the actual weather in the test year had been exactly normal.  The use of 
3 
these adjustments in the allocation process provides a more robust cost of service result 
4 
which can then be used as a reasonable foundation for the Company’s proposed rate 
5 
design. 
6 
7 
Q. 
Were test year sales and revenues used in your cost study adjusted for weather? 
8 
A. 
Yes, they were.  The test year was colder than normal resulting in a $162,609 reduction 
9 
in firm rate revenues.  The calculations for both weather adjusted ccf sales and associated 
10 
revenues for the test year are included in Schedule PMN-2.  Each page contains monthly 
11 
usage, degree days, and a detailed calculation of the weather adjustment.  The summary 
12 
results of the weather adjustment on Schedule PMN-2 are contained on pages 21 to 23.  
13 
14

ACCOUNTING COST OF SERVICE STUDY 
1 
Allocated Cost of Service Study  
2 
Q. 
Would you briefly define an Allocated Cost of Service Study?
3 
A. 
The cost to serve the customers of any utility company consists generally of operating 
4 
expenses and return.  For a historical test period, these costs are on record and the overall 
5 
cost to serve the collective customers of the utility may be readily established.  On the 
6 
other hand, the unique cost to serve customers of the various service classifications is 
7 
much less apparent.  Costs can vary significantly between customer classes depending 
8 
upon the nature of their demands upon the system and the facilities required to serve 
9 
them.  The purpose of an Allocated Cost of Service Study is to assign or allocate each 
10 
relevant component of cost on an appropriate basis in order to determine the proper cost 
11 
to serve.  The result is a cost matrix displaying for each cost category the detailed costs 
12 
of serving each customer class in this study.

18 
operations, it was possible to treat each element of Rate Base, Revenue and Operating 
19 
Expense in detail and to assign or allocate each item to the customer classes.  The 
20 
complete detailed allocation process is presented in Schedule PMN-6.  Specific pro 
21 
forma adjustments to this test year are discussed in detail in the Company’s testimony

13

14

15 
service study begins with rate base and continues with revenues, operating expenses, 
16 
taxes, and the computation of a labor allocator. The cost model includes three additional 
17 
pieces, a summary of costs to serve, a list of the allocation factors employed in the study 
18 
and a revenue requirements section.  The horizontal portion consists of the assignment of 
19 
all costs to each of the Company’s customer classes.

Rate Base Allocation

8

9

10

11

13 
14 
 Transmission Plant and demand-related Distribution Plant were then allocated to

16 
PMN-6. 
17 
18 
Q. 
Mr. Normand, please describe the allocation of Distribution Mains Acct 376 to 
19 
customer classes. 
20 
A. 
The Distribution Mains account has been classified as demand (57.66%) and customer 
21 
(42.34%) using the results of a minimum-size system analysis.  The minimum-size 
22 
system method uses a mathematical approach and relies heavily on current installation 
23 
372


--- Page 373 ---
UK 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 12 of 21 
costs and practices to derive a minimum cost per foot for each size of mains.  The 
1 
minimum or customer related cost for mains is presented in Schedule PMN-10 and was 
2 
calculated as follows: 
3 
1.  2020 Total Main Cost = Three-year average (2018, 2019, & 2020) current cost per 
4 
foot of each main size * Number of feet of each main size used in the analysis (2’’, 4”, 
5 
6”, 8”, 12”). 
6 
2.   Customer related main cost = Average minimum current cost of 2” main * Number 
7 
of feet found in each main size (2’’, 4”, 6”, 8”, 12”).  
8 
3.  Customer related percentage (42.34%) = Customer related main cost / 2020 Total 
9 
Main Cost.  
10 
4.  Demand related percentage (57.66%) = 1 – Customer related percentage. 
11 
The demand portion of mains is allocated using a design day allocation factor and the 
12 
customer portion of mains is allocated using the annual number of customers by class.

5

How did you approach the task of rate design in this case?
6 
A.

7 
test period of March 31, 2021 provided the basis or starting point for all of the proposed 
8

9 
 10 
Q.   
Was there a logical progression in your efforts to perform the rate design?
11 
A. 
My rate design efforts were performed in three discrete steps.   First, I determined the 
12 
total costs incurred to serve each customer class using the adjusted historical test year, 
13 
Schedule PMN-6.  Next, I examined the accounting cost of service study at the 
14 
Company’s uniform ROR (equalized annual increase) and compared these results to the 
15 
revenues currently produced by each customer class. Due to the Company’s overall 
16 
increase level, I propose a uniform class increase with emphasis on increasing the fixed 
17 
portion of customer charges closer to costs in order to reduce existing subsidies for 
18 
smaller customers.

17

18 
typical or normal circumstances.  The Company has identified specific pro forma 
19 
adjustments to the test year to reflect the expenses that normally would be anticipated in 
20 
the test year, based on those changes which are known and measurable at the present 
21 
time.  However, another important adjustment is the Company’s ccf sales which are 
22 
weather sensitive.  Even small variations in weather can have a material impact on the 
23 
387


--- Page 388 ---

Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 6 of 21 
sales and related revenues, especially for a gas utility.  The weather normalization 
1 
adjustment is targeted to identify the change in sales and revenue that would have been 
2 
anticipated if the actual weather in the test year had been exactly normal.  The use of 
3 
these adjustments in the allocation process provides a more robust cost of service result 
4 
which can then be used as a reasonable foundation for the Company’s proposed rate 
5 
design.

ACCOUNTING COST OF SERVICE STUDY 
1 
Allocated Cost of Service Study  
2 
Q. 
Would you briefly define an Allocated Cost of Service Study?
3 
A. 
The cost to serve the customers of any utility company consists generally of operating 
4 
expenses and return.  For a historical test period, these costs are on record and the overall 
5 
cost to serve the collective customers of the utility may be readily established.  On the 
6 
other hand, the unique cost to serve customers of the various service classifications is 
7 
much less apparent.  Costs can vary significantly between customer classes depending 
8 
upon the nature of their demands upon the system and the facilities required to serve 
9 
them.  The purpose of an Allocated Cost of Service Study is to assign or allocate each 
10 
relevant component of cost on an appropriate basis in order to determine the proper cost 
11 
to serve.  The result is a cost matrix displaying for each cost category the detailed costs 
12 
of serving each customer class in this study. 
13 
 14 
Q. 
Please describe the procedure that you used in preparing your Allocated Cost of 
15 
Service Study?
16 
A. 
Through the application of a computerized microcomputer cost model developed by 
17 
Management Applications Consulting specifically for Corning Natural Gas Corporation's 
18 
operations, it was possible to treat each element of Rate Base, Revenue and Operating 
19 
Expense in detail and to assign or allocate each item to the customer classes.  The 
20 
complete detailed allocation process is presented in Schedule PMN-6.  Specific pro 
21 
forma adjustments to this test year are discussed in detail in the Company’s testimony 
22 
390


--- Page 391 ---
MO( 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 9 of 21 
and have been identified in the detailed cost of service study presented in Schedule 
1 
PMN-6. 
2 
3 
Q. 
Please summarize your cost of service study.
4 
A. 
Schedule PMN-3 shows the summary results of class cost of service study based upon 
5 
present rates and a historical 12-month period ended March 31, 2021.  Schedule PMN-4 
6 
shows a similar summary of the cost of service study where existing and calculated 
7 
uniform target rate of return revenue levels for each customer class are developed based 
8 
on the adjusted historical test year ended March 31, 2021.  The detailed cost of service 
9 
study which supports Schedule PMN-4 is provided in Schedule PMN-6). 
10

Description of Cost Model 
12 
Q. 
How does the computerized cost model operate?
13 
A. 
The cost model is essentially a cost matrix.  The vertical dimension of the study consists 
14 
of the costs to serve as provided by the Company.  The development of the cost of 
15 
service study begins with rate base and continues with revenues, operating expenses, 
16 
taxes, and the computation of a labor allocator. The cost model includes three additional 
17 
pieces, a summary of costs to serve, a list of the allocation factors employed in the study 
18 
and a revenue requirements section.  The horizontal portion consists of the assignment of 
19 
all costs to each of the Company’s customer classes.  
20 
 21 
Each page, starting with page 1 has an important column immediately preceding the 
22 
numerical data marked “ALLOC”, an abbreviation for ALLOCATOR.  The ALLOC 
23

column contains an acronym to indicate the allocation factor used to allocate the costs 
1 
shown in the Total Company Column to each customer class.  A tabulation of these 
2 
allocators in absolute form, typically total dollars or volumes and as a percent of total has 
3 
been provided at the end of the study beginning on page 41 in Schedule PMN-6. 
4 
 5 
Using these allocation factors, costs shown in the Total Company column that were not

year provided by the Company.

Rate Base Allocation

8

9

10 
Company’s key distribution service areas from its pipeline suppliers.  Distribution plant 
11

12

13 
14 
 Transmission Plant and demand-related Distribution Plant were then allocated to 
15 
customer classes using the Design Day factors shown on pages 41 and 42 of Schedule 
16

17 
18 
Q. 
Mr. Normand, please describe the allocation of Distribution Mains Acct 376 to 
19 
customer classes. 
20 
A. 
The Distribution Mains account has been classified as demand (57.66%) and customer 
21 
(42.34%) using the results of a minimum-size system analysis.  The minimum-size 
22 
system method uses a mathematical approach and relies heavily on current installation 
23 
393


--- Page 394 ---
UK 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 12 of 21 
costs and practices to derive a minimum cost per foot for each size of mains.  The 
1 
minimum or customer related cost for mains is presented in Schedule PMN-10 and was 
2 
calculated as follows: 
3 
1.  2020 Total Main Cost = Three-year average (2018, 2019, & 2020) current cost per 
4 
foot of each main size * Number of feet of each main size used in the analysis (2’’, 4”, 
5 
6”, 8”, 12”). 
6 
2.   Customer related main cost = Average minimum current cost of 2” main * Number 
7 
of feet found in each main size (2’’, 4”, 6”, 8”, 12”).  
8 
3.  Customer related percentage (42.34%) = Customer related main cost / 2020 Total 
9 
Main Cost.  
10 
4.  Demand related percentage (57.66%) = 1 – Customer related percentage. 
11 
The demand portion of mains is allocated using a design day allocation factor and the 
12 
customer portion of mains is allocated using the annual number of customers by class.

RATE DESIGN 
5 
Q. 
How did you approach the task of rate design in this case?
6 
A.
The cost of service summary results presented in Schedule PMN-6 for CNG historical 
7 
test period of March 31, 2021 provided the basis or starting point for all of the proposed 
8 
rate designs presented on Schedule PMN-5.   
9 
 10 
Q.   
Was there a logical progression in your efforts to perform the rate design?
11 
A. 
My rate design efforts were performed in three discrete steps.   First, I determined the 
12 
total costs incurred to serve each customer class using the adjusted historical test year, 
13 
Schedule PMN-6.  Next, I examined the accounting cost of service study at the 
14 
Company’s uniform ROR (equalized annual increase) and compared these results to the 
15 
revenues currently produced by each customer class. Due to the Company’s overall 
16 
increase level, I propose a uniform class increase with emphasis on increasing the fixed 
17 
portion of customer charges closer to costs in order to reduce existing subsidies for 
18 
smaller customers.

Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 8 of 8 
Q. 
Is a proper Net Salvage estimate an important aspect to establishing reasonable and 
1 
equitable depreciation accrual rates? 
2 
A. 
Yes it is.  Net salvage is an important cost that must be recovered in an equitable manner 
3 
over the useful life of an asset from those customers who benefit from the use and service 
4 
of an asset.  To defer the proper recovery of these costs over a realistic useful life until 
5 
much later at retirement, or underestimating these levels, will introduce a subsidy to 
6 
existing customers by the recovery of these costs from only future customers who may in 
7 
fact only use an asset for a very small portion of its life. 
8

A. 
Yes, it does.

COMPARABLE RETURN STANDARD 
Q.
Are authorized returns in other jurisdictions a relevant benchmark to 
11 
evaluate the reasonableness of the ROE recommendation of Staff? 
12 
A.
Yes.  The Hope and Bluefield cases establish that authorized ROEs be 
13 
comparable to other investments of commensurate risk. Therefore, the 
14 
regulatory decisions of other commissions provide a basic test of 
15 
reasonableness and a benchmark that investors consider in assessing the 
16 
authorized ROE of one utility against the returns available from other 
17 
regulated utilities with comparable risk. 
18 
19 
422


--- Page 423 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall 
Page 9 of 121
Q.
In your opinion, is the equity return recommendation of Staff 
1 
consistent with the comparable return standard? 
2 
A.
No, it is not.  While Staff references the fair return standard5, Staff has not 
3 
demonstrated how their ROE recommendation for Corning Gas is supported 
4 
by the authorized ROEs for other natural gas distribution companies across 
5 
the U.S. or expected market conditions. Therefore, Staff has not developed 
6 
an appropriate analysis to determine if their recommendation meets the 
7 
comparable return standard, a standard that they have noted is a key 
8 
principle in determining the ROE. In my view, Staff’s recommendation of 
9 
9.00 percent does not meet the comparable return standard outlined in the 
10 
Hope and Bluefield decisions for establishing the authorized ROE for the 
11 
Company.

Q.
What effect will inflation have on long-term interest rates?  
14 
A.
Inflation and the Federal Reserve’s normalization of monetary policy will 
15 
likely result in increases in long-term interest rates.  Specifically, inflation 
16 
reduces the purchasing power of the future interest payments an investor 
17 
expects to receive over the duration of the bond.  This risk increases the 
18 
longer the duration of the bond.  As a result, if investors expect increased 
19 
levels of inflation, they will require higher yields to compensate for the 
20 
increased risk of inflation which means interest rates will increase.

10

16

17

18

Generally, the mean result of an analysis is more susceptible to outlier data 
2 
points than the median result because each individual result is given equal 
3

4 
potential presence of outlier data points.  Therefore, while Staff has 
5

6

7

8

9 
results of the DCF model were not reflecting investors’ forward-looking 
10 
expectations. Had Staff recognized this circumstance and worked to remedy

12

13 
specified with forward-looking inputs, it would not be necessary to change 
14 
the measure of central tendency to achieve a higher result, as Staff has done.

A.
PROXY GROUP COMPOSITION
10 
Q.
What is your position with respect to the proxy group composition? 
11 
A.
An appropriately constructed proxy group consists of companies that are 
12 
comparable in business and financial risk to Corning Gas.  The importance 
13 
of selecting a proxy group that is similar in overall financial and business 
14 
risk to the subject company was endorsed by the United States Court of 
15 
Appeals for the District of Columbia (the “DC Circuit”) in the Petal Gas 
16 
Storage decision.  The DC Circuit acknowledged that the goal of a proxy 
17 
group is to rely on companies that possess similar risk to the subject 
18 
company for the determination of the cost of equity: 
19 
That proxy group arrangements must be risk-
20 
appropriate is the common theme in each argument.  
21 
The principle is well-established.  See Hope Natural Gas 
22 
Co., 320 U.S. at 603 (“[T]he return to the equity owner 
23 
should be commensurate with returns on investments in 
24 
other enterprises having corresponding risks.”); CAPP 
25 
I, 254 F.3d at 293 (“[A] utility must offer a risk-adjusted 
26 
expected rate of return sufficient to attract investors.”).  
27 
446


--- Page 447 ---
Rebuttal Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall 
Page 33 of 121
The principle captures what proxy groups do, namely, 
1 
provide market-determined stock and dividend figures 
2 
from public companies comparable to a target company 
3 
for which those figures are unavailable.  CAPP I, 254 
4 
F.3d at 293–94.  Market-determined stock figures 
5 
reflect a company’s risk level and, when combined with 
6 
dividend values, permit calculation of the “risk-adjusted 
7 
expected rate of return sufficient to attract investors.” 
8 
*** 
9 
What matters is that the overall proxy group 
10 
arrangement makes sense in terms of relative risk and, 
11 
even more importantly, in terms of the statutory 
12 
command to set “just and reasonable” rates, 15 U.S.C. § 
13 
717c, that are “commensurate with returns on 
14 
investments in other enterprises having corresponding 
15 
risks” and “sufficient to assure confidence in the 
16 
financial integrity of the enterprise . . . [and] maintain 
17 
its credit and . . . attract capital,” Hope Natural Gas Co., 
18 
320 U.S. at 603.35
19 
20 
Consistent with the DC Circuit’s decision, we have selected a proxy group 
21 
of companies with comparable investment risk to Corning Gas.  In contrast, 
22 
Staff applied less stringent screening criteria, which result in a larger, but 
23 
less comparable proxy group.

17

18

20

5

6

7

14

21

6

11

12

13 
which is ultimately what determines the ROE to the investor.  As discussed 
14 
in our Direct Testimony, dividends are based on management decisions 
15 
related to cash management and other factors, and therefore dividend 
16 
growth rates are less likely to accurately reflect investors’ growth 
17

18
