6 
7 
Finally, from a practical perspective, the ROE that is approved by the 
8 
Commission will be the return that will be reflected in rates over the rate 
9 
period, until such time as another rate proceeding is concluded.  It is 
10 
important to reflect investors’ expectations of returns over that time period.  
11 
Therefore, we conclude that it is appropriate to consider consensus 
12 
estimates of investors’ expectation of yields on Treasury Bonds in the 
13 
CAPM analysis.

doubling its Sharpe ratio, but also resurrects it in the 
16 
1980s and 1990s when it is otherwise conspicuously 
17 
absent, restores a more linear relation between size and 
18 
average returns (i.e., no longer concentrated among the 
19 
tiniest firms), revives the returns to size outside of 
20 
January while simultaneously diminishing the returns to 
21 
size in January (making it more uniform across months), 
22 
and uncovers a larger size effect in almost two dozen 
23 
other international equity markets (where size has been 
24 
notably weak). This stronger size effect controlling for 
25 
other factors, including the market and other risk-based 
26 
factors, is inconsistent with standard theories of asset 
27 
pricing.119
28 
29 
The findings of Asness, et. al. are important because they not only provide 
30 
further support for the small size premium but they also show that many of 
31 
the irregularities noted in the past seem to be the result of quality and “junk” 
32 
firms being included in the same sample.  The latter conclusion is important 
33 
in this proceeding because we have developed a sample of quality firms in 
34 
119
Asness, Clifford, et al. “Size Matters, If You Control Your Junk.” Journal of 
Financial Economics, vol. 129, no. 3, Sept. 2018, pp. 479–509.

the proxy group with each having a credit rating of investment grade or

above.  Therefore, it is appropriate to consider the small size premium in

5

6 
A.
Yes.  By relying on the Zero Beta CAPM to calculate the ROE for Corning 
7 
Gas, Staff has implicitly acknowledged that a size premium could exist for 
8 
the Company.  As acknowledged by Staff, the purpose of the Zero Beta 
9 
CAPM is to account for the fact that the risk return relationship may be 
10 
flatter than is indicated by the CAPM which means that the CAPM may 
11 
underestimate the required return for companies that have a Beta coefficient 
12 
less than one such as utilities.120 The risk return relationship is flatter than 
13 
indicated by the traditional form of the CAPM because the traditional form 
14 
of the CAPM does not capture the effect on the required return of additional 
15 
risk factors such as size. As Dr. Morin noted:  
16 
As discussed in the previous section, several finance

19

20

Q.
What are your conclusions regarding the effect of the Company’s small 
1 
size on its cost of equity? 
2 
A.
We continue to believe that a small size adjustment is appropriate for 
3 
Corning Gas.  As described in our Direct Testimony, smaller utility 
4 
companies are less able than larger utility companies to withstand adverse 
5 
events such as the reduction of demand due to macroeconomic conditions 
6 
because they have smaller customer bases, more limited financial resources, 
7 
and less diversification.123   Corning Gas is no exception.  Other regulators, 
8 
such as FERC and those in Alaska and Minnesota, have recognized the 
9 
effect of size on utility companies’ risk.124   While Staff references two 
10 
academic articles that oppose the use of a size premium, the referenced 
11 
articles are of limited relevance in this case because, as noted above, the 
12 
concerns raised in the articles have each been addressed in academic articles 
13 
which provide support for the use of the size premium.   Additionally, there 
14 
have been numerous studies that have provided support for the use of a size 
15 
premium adjustment to account for the additional risk associated with small 
16 
size in the regulated utility sector. Therefore, it is reasonable to adjust the 
17 
results of the traditional cost of equity models by 50 basis points to reflect 
18 
the incremental risks that Corning Gas faces due to its small size. 
19

Q.  Has Corning made any changes to its insurance 
1

9 
Q. 
 What is a captive insurer?  
10 
A. 
A captive insurer is an insurance company that 
11 
is wholly owned and controlled by its insured 
12 
entities.   
13 
Q. 
Please, explain group captive insurance.   
14 
A. 
Group captive insurance is provided by a group 
15 
of individuals or entities that jointly own a 
16 
captive insurance company.  In effect, the 
17 
policy holders are collectively self-insuring. 
18 
Q. 
What is the Panel’s understanding of how group 
19 
captive insurance works?  
20 
A. 
An accepted member of a group captive must 
21 
contribute capital to become a member.  In 
22 
addition to the capital contribution, a member 
23 
is charged yearly premiums that are determined 
24 
562


--- Page 563 ---
Case 21-G-0394 
 
STAFF ACCOUNTING PANEL 
 
 
27 
 
by individual risk, recent loss experienced, and 
1 
business risk.  Any unused premiums may 
2 
eventually be returned to members.  Members may 
3 
earn a return on unused premiums and/or capital 
4 
contributions which may be distributed to 
5 
members through dividends.  However, the 
6 
member’s capital is at risk for investment 
7 
losses if the group captive goes bankrupt or if 
8 
there are other losses on its investments. 
9 
Q. 
Panel, please describe Corning’s group captive 
10 
insurance company, Presidio, Ltd. 
11 
A. 
Presidio, Ltd. is a group captive insurance 
12 
company comprised of 297 members and is based in 
13 
the Cayman Islands.  Access to membership is by 
14 
approved application and stock purchase for 
15 
$36,000.  The members are responsible for 
16 
premiums which consist of three parts: Fund A, 
17 
Fund B, and operating costs.  
18 
Q. 
Describe Fund A.  
19 
A. 
Fund A is dedicated to claims up to $125,000.  
20 
In essence this is self-insurance where any 
21 
claim within this loss criteria is paid out of a 
22 
member’s Fund A.  Any remaining amount in the 
23 
fund after the insurance year ends is kept in 
24 
563


--- Page 564 ---
Case 21-G-0394 
 
STAFF ACCOUNTING PANEL 
 
 
28 
 
the fund, earns a return, and can be returned to 
1 
Corning as a dividend when the insurance year is 
2 
closed.  If there are multiple Fund A claims in 
3 
an insurance year, and the total of those claims 
4 
exceed Corning’s Fund A annual premium, the 
5 
captive will continue to pay those claims, but 
6 
Corning will be required to repay the captive 
7 
for this excess amount over the next three 
8 
years.  However, this potential liability for 
9 
excess claims is capped at an amount equal to 
10 
the Fund A premium.  In other words, Corning 
11 
only bears financial responsibility for total 
12 
Fund A claims up to two times the Fund A 
13 
premium.  Any claims beyond this amount will be 
14 
shared by the other members of the captive, 
15 
without reimbursement. 
16 
Q. 
Describe Fund B.  
17 
A. 
Fund B is dedicated to claims between $125,000 
18 
and $350,000.  Like Fund A, this is essentially 
19 
self-insurance where any claim within this loss 
20 
criteria is paid out of Fund B.  Any remaining 
21 
amount in the fund after the insurance year ends 
22 
is kept in the fund, earns a return, and can be 
23 
returned to Corning as a dividend when the 
24 
564


--- Page 565 ---
Case 21-G-0394 
 
STAFF ACCOUNTING PANEL 
 
 
29 
 
insurance year is closed.  If there are multiple 
1 
claims between $125,000 and $350,000 in an 
2 
insurance year, and the total of these claims 
3 
exceed Corning’s Fund B annual premium, the 
4 
captive will continue to pay those claims.  
5 
However, unlike Fund A, Corning is not required 
6 
to repay the captive for these excess claims.  
7 
Instead, all excess claims will be shared by the 
8 
other members of the captive, without 
9 
reimbursement.

How are claims between $350,000 and $1 million

15 
available for all members of the group captive, 
16 
and the cost for this reinsurance is included in 
17 
the operating expense portion of each member’s 
18

Paycheck Protection Program Loan 
1 
Q. 
What is the Paycheck Protection Program? 
2 
A. 
On March 17, 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, 
3 
and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) was 
4 
enacted.  The intent of the CARES Act is to 
5 
soften the economic impact of the COVID-19 
6 
pandemic.  The CARES Act includes, among other 
7 
things the Payroll Protection Program (PPP), 
8 
which provided small businesses employing 500 
9 
people or less with loans to cover up to eight 
10 
weeks of payroll costs, paid sick, medical or 
11 
family leave, mortgage interest, rent, utility 
12 
payments, and interest on pre-existing debts.  
13 
The June 5, 2020 Paycheck Protection Program 
14 
Flexibility Act extended the duration of PPP 
15 
loans from eight to 24 weeks, and also permitted 
16 
borrowers to spend just 60%, rather than 75%, of 
17 
the loan proceeds on payroll.  Repayment of the 
18 
loan under the PPP may be forgiven and converted 
19 
into a grant after two years if the recipient 
20 
meets certain conditions.  These conditions 
21 
include the requirement that the loan be used 
22 
for payroll, that employee pay is not reduced by 
23 
more than 25%, and there is no reduction in full 
24

FAIR RATE OF RETURN 
6 
Q. 
Earlier, the Panel mentioned that the fair rate 
7 
of return that it recommends will be used to 
8 
establish the Company’s revenue requirement.  
9 
Please explain what the Panel means by revenue 
10 
requirement. 
11 
A. 
In the context of Commission rate proceedings, 
12 
the revenue requirement is the dollar amount 
13 
required by a company to provide service during 
14 
a rate year.  It is the amount that will allow 
15 
the company to recover all of its reasonably 
16 
expected operating costs, including taxes and 
17 
depreciation.  In addition, the revenue 
18 
requirement includes a fair return that will 
19 
allow the utility the opportunity to recover the 
20 
cost of funds supplied to it by investors.  The 
21 
funds provided by these investors are necessary 
22 
for the company to finance its long-term utility 
23 
assets and working capital requirements, which 
24 
633


--- Page 634 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
9 
 
in the rate-setting context are referred to as 
1 
its “rate base.” 
2 
Q. 
Generally speaking, what is a fair rate of 
3 
return for a regulated utility? 
4 
A. 
A fair rate of return for a regulated utility is 
5 
one that enables it to provide safe and adequate 
6 
service to its customers, while at the same time 
7 
assuring the company continuing support in the 
8 
capital markets for both its debt and equity 
9 
securities, at terms that are reasonable given 
10 
the company’s risk.  The fair rate of return, 
11 
therefore, allows the utility to recover its 
12 
prudently incurred cost of debt while providing 
13 
its common equity investors the opportunity to 
14 
earn a return that is commensurate with the risk 
15 
of their investment. 
16 
Q. 
How is a fair rate of return calculated? 
17 
A. 
The fair rate of return for a utility company is 
18 
calculated as the weighted average cost of the 
19 
individual components of its expected 
20 
capitalization during the rate year.  The two 
21 
primary sources are long-term debt and common 
22 
equity.  Customer deposits, while typically a 
23 
very small component, are almost always 
24 
634


--- Page 635 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
10 
 
reflected in the expected capitalization as well 
1 
because they are a relatively permanent and 
2 
stable source of capital employed by utilities.  
3 
Preferred stock and short-term debt are 
4 
sometimes a source of capital as well, although 
5 
in smaller proportions than either long-term 
6 
debt or common equity.  Since the Commission 
7 
uses a fully forecast rate year, it is also 
8 
important that the rate year capitalization 
9 
reflects the utility’s projected capital 
10 
requirements and is consistent with the goal of 
11 
achieving the optimal cost of capital, 
12 
particularly as it relates to the use of 
13 
leverage. 
14 
Q. 
How are the cost rates of the individual cost 
15 
components of capitalization typically 
16 
calculated? 
17 
A. 
The cost rates associated with a utility’s long-
18 
debt, short-term debt, and customer deposits are 
19 
relatively straightforward to ascertain.  The 
20 
embedded cost of debt, both long-term and short-
21 
term, can be readily calculated by examining the 
22 
contractual terms; i.e., the interest payments 
23 
for the debt.  The projected impact of the cost 
24 
635


--- Page 636 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
11 
 
of any new or incremental debt, however, 
1 
requires estimates using relevant market data.  
2 
The cost rate for customer deposits is simply a 
3 
matter of applying the cost rate that is 
4 
currently prescribed by the Commission.  The 
5 
cost of common equity, however, is neither 
6 
contractual nor prescribed by the Commission.  
7 
Its calculation is further complicated by the 
8 
fact that it cannot be directly observed, and 
9 
instead requires estimation and the opinion of 
10 
analysts.  
11 
Q. 
Is the cost of common equity typically more 
12 
expensive than the cost of long-term debt for a 
13 
utility?   
14 
A. 
Yes.  Even though both lenders and common equity 
15 
investors supply the utility with the funds it 
16 
needs to build and operate its system, the 
17 
common equity investors only earn a return after 
18 
the payment of all other expenses.  Because 
19 
these investors run the risk that their achieved 
20 
returns will not meet their expectations, the 
21 
return required by common equity investors is 
22 
usually higher than that of the utility’s long-
23 
term debt holders.  Exceptions may exist during 
24 
636


--- Page 637 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
12 
 
periods of disturbances in the market, such as 
1 
during the recessionary period of 1980 to 1982, 
2 
at which point the economy was beset with very 
3 
high inflation and volatile interest rates.  
4 
During that time, utility bond yields were at 
5 
least as high as the equity returns the 
6 
Commission allowed, and far above the returns 
7 
allowed by most state regulatory commissions.   
8 
Q. 
How can a utility’s cost of common equity be 
9 
measured? 
10 
A. 
The return requirements of a utility’s common 
11 
equity investors can only be gleaned through a 
12 
cost of equity analysis.  Generally, the 
13 
Commission has favored market-based 
14 
methodologies, such as the Discounted Cash Flow 
15 
(DCF) and the Capital Asset Pricing Model 
16 
(CAPM), to estimate the return required by 
17 
common equity investors.

Q. 
Why is this significant? 
3 
A. 
Nearly all utility holding companies have both 
4 
regulated businesses, as well as unregulated 
5 
businesses.  Given the significant differences 
6 
in business risk between the unregulated 
7 
operations and the regulated utilities, there 
8

9

10 
particular degree of risk.  Rational financing 
11 
policies would assure that the higher business 
12 
risk activities of a diversified entity are 
13 
offset by the deployment of lower risk financial 
14 
policies than would be needed to finance its 
15 
lower business risk segments.   
16 
Q. 
Please explain, in general, the concept of 
17 
business risk and financial risk. 
18 
A. 
Business risk is the risk inherent in a 
19 
company’s operation and reflects the risk that 
20 
it will fail to achieve its expected financial 
21 
performance.  It is affected by factors such as 
22 
a company’s sensitivity to the overall economy, 
23 
the level of competition it faces, and the 
24 
648


--- Page 649 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
24 
 
diversity of its customer and/or supplier bases.  
1 
Generally speaking, long-established utilities 
2 
tend to have lower levels of business risk as 
3 
compared to other businesses.  Financial risk, 
4 
on the other hand, is the risk a company faces 
5 
due to the amount of leverage employed to 
6 
finance its capital investments.   
7 
Q. 
Given the typical variances in business risk 
8 
between established utilities and other 
9 
businesses, what capitalization differences 
10 
would be expected between them? 
11 
A. 
As a result of their low business risk nature, 
12 
established utilities are generally able to 
13 
employ significantly higher levels of financial 
14 
risk than other businesses and still be 
15 
considered creditworthy.  Other businesses would 
16 
be expected to have relatively larger equity 
17 
“cushions” to protect against variances in 
18 
earnings impacting their ability to meet debt 
19 
obligations.  Essentially, this means that these 
20 
businesses typically need to maintain lower 
21 
levels of financial leverage than established 
22 
utilities in order to be seen as a worthwhile 
23 
credit risk to a potential lender.

Q.

11

20 
holders do.  This makes it difficult to judge 
21 
the extent to which Holdings’ preferred equity 
22 
can truly be considered an equity position, and 
23 
accordingly, the extent of its financial risk.

Q. 
The Panel mentioned earlier that Corning does

A. 
Sufficient ring-fencing is generally achieved by 
15 
restricting the shifting of assets and 
16 
liabilities between a parent company and its 
17 
subsidiary.  This is generally accomplished 
18 
through a variety of restrictive covenants.  
19 
These include a minimum equity ratio, a 
20 
prohibition on cross-default provisions, and a 
21 
restriction on comingling funds with affiliates. 
22 
 
 
It is also common for New York State 
23 
utilities to have the following requirements: 1) 
24 
653


--- Page 654 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
29 
 
The utility subsidiary must issue its own long-
1 
term debt; 2) It must maintain a minimum credit 
2 
rating separate from that of its parent company; 
3 
3) The company must establish a single purpose 
4 
entity, commonly known as a golden share 
5 
preferred stock, to prevent a parent-induced 
6 
bankruptcy of the utility; and, 4) The company’s 
7 
general counsel must issue a non-consolidation 
8 
opinion demonstrating that satisfactory legal 
9 
and credit separation between the utility and 
10 
its affiliates has been achieved.  These 
11 
measures are in place for Niagara Mohawk Power 
12 
Corp., Brooklyn Union Gas Company., Keyspan Gas 
13 
East Corp., New York State Electric & Gas Corp., 
14 
Rochester Gas & Electric Corp., and Central 
15 
Hudson Electric & Gas Corp.  A chart 
16 
illustrating this information can be found in 
17 
Exhibit__(FP-7).

SUMMARY OF ROE RECOMMENDATION 
4 
Q. 
What methodology did the Panel use to determine 
5 
its recommended ROE for Corning? 
6 
A. 
We estimated the cost of equity for a proxy 
7 
group of electric and gas utility holding 
8 
companies, using a DCF analysis, weighted two-
9 
thirds, and the average of two CAPM analyses, 
10 
weighted one-third.  As is Staff’s typical 
11 
practice, in order to determine whether an 
12 
adjustment to the proxy group’s cost of equity 
13 
is warranted, we examined the differences in 
14 
business risk and financial risk between Corning 
15 
and our proxy group.  After our thorough review 
16 
of the collective risks of our proxy group and 
17 
Corning, we have determined that our 9.00% ROE 
18 
recommendation is fair and reasonable.  
19 
Q. 
Please explain why the Panel specifically 
20 
recommends that the DCF methodology be given a 
21 
two-thirds weighting and the CAPM result a one-
22 
third weighting? 
23 
A. 
Over the past 25 years, the DCF has been the 
24 
670


--- Page 671 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
46 
 
principal cost of equity methodology in New York 
1 
State.  In fact, the Commission has consistently 
2 
used the same two-thirds DCF and one-third CAPM 
3 
weightings since the recommended decision in the 
4 
Generic Finance Proceeding (Case 91-M-0509) was 
5 
issued on July 19, 1994.  Since that time, in 
6 
every major rate case, Staff has advocated that 
7 
the CAPM be weighted less than the DCF in the 
8 
overall ROE calculation.  In fact, Staff 
9 
testimony addressing ROE has consistently noted 
10 
the numerous reasons why the DCF has been and 
11 
should continue to be, the preferred 
12 
methodology. 
13 
 
 
Estimating the cost of equity requires 
14 
using methodologies that are not perfect.  Of 
15 
all the approaches available, however, the DCF 
16 
and the CAPM are by far the least flawed, and, 
17 
between the two, the DCF is superior.  In fact, 
18 
the Commission has noted the relative strengths 
19 
of the DCF methodology in many of its previous 
20

21 
Rate Order issued October 18, 2007, in Case 06-

E-1433, Orange and Rockland Utilities, Inc.,

the Commission stated that “the method offers 
24 
671


--- Page 672 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
47 
 
the significant benefit of reliance on readily 
1 
available, objective data to measure an 
2 
indicator of real importance to investors.”   
3 
 
 
We will demonstrate the strengths and 
4 
reasonableness of our two-stage DCF methodology 
5 
in this testimony.  We will also demonstrate 
6 
that our forward-looking application of the CAPM 
7 
continues to produce a reasonable check on our 
8 
DCF methodology and, as such, should continue to 
9 
be accorded a one-third weighting.

USE OF PROXY GROUP 
11 
Q. 
Why is a proxy group used to estimate Corning’s 
12 
cost of equity? 
13 
A. 
The use of a proxy group to determine the cost 
14 
of equity is necessary for several reasons. 
15 
First, the Company’s common stock is not 
16 
publicly traded, and, thus, direct DCF and CAPM 
17 
analyses of the Company are not possible. 
18 
Equally important is that DCF analyses for 
19 
individual companies rely on equity analysts’ 
20 
estimates of growth, and those estimates, by 
21 
their nature, could be biased or potentially 
22 
inaccurate.  Similarly, beta determinations used 
23 
in the CAPM methodology are based on historical 
24 
672


--- Page 673 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
48 
 
observations that, due to circumstances such as 
1 
corporate restructurings or industry 
2 
transformations, may not be representative of 
3 
the level of earnings volatility expected in the 
4 
future.  However, by employing a sufficiently 
5 
large proxy group of similarly situated 
6 
companies in our analyses, we can minimize the 
7 
undesirable effects of bias, both upward and 
8 
downward, or inaccurate estimates for any one 
9 
company.  
10 
Q. 
What are the most important considerations for 
11 
selecting a proxy group? 
12 
A. 
First, it is important to determine the specific 
13 
industry classification of the subject company 
14 
to identify its true peers.  Second, once the 
15 
appropriate group of peer companies is 
16 
established, careful consideration must be given 
17 
to determining the appropriate screening 
18 
criteria to establish a group of companies that 
19 
is both sufficiently large and of similar risk 
20 
to the company in question.  A careful balance 
21 
must be struck between these two potentially 
22 
conflicting goals.  While the objective is to 
23 
select a group of companies whose risks closely 
24 
673


--- Page 674 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
49 
 
match those of the subject company, it is also 
1 
important that the proxy group is large enough 
2 
to provide sufficient confidence in the results.  
3 
The greater the number of suitable companies 
4 
that can be found, the less sensitive the 
5 
overall cost of equity estimate will be to the 
6 
fluctuations or irregularities in the data 
7 
related to any one particular company. 
8

DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW (DCF) METHODOLOGY 
9 
Q.  Please explain the basic theory underlying the 
10 
DCF methodology. 
11 
A.  The DCF approach can be applied to any 
12 
investment instrument that has an intrinsic 
13 
value.  The DCF approach, as it relates to 
14 
common stock, recognizes that companies create 
15 
value for their stockholders by using their 
16 
earnings in a number of ways, the most important 
17 
of which, by far, is through the payment of cash 
18 
dividends.  Alternatively, earnings that are 
19 
retained by companies can be used to create 
20 
value by investing in capital projects designed 
21 
to increase future profits.  The retained 
22 
earnings can also create value by retiring debt, 
23 
which reduces interest expense, thereby 
24 
685


--- Page 686 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
61 
 
resulting in greater cash flow available to 
1 
stockholders, and by buying back some of the 
2 
Company’s common stock, which increases future 
3 
earnings on a per-share basis. 
4 
Q. 
What principles support the DCF? 
5 
A. 
It is important to note that, while earnings 
6 
drive companies’ dividend payout policies, the 
7 
value of the companies’ common stock is equal to 
8 
the present value of all future dividends.  This 
9 
is because the earnings that are retained will 
10 
only have value to the stockholder when they are 
11 
paid as dividends in the future.  Underlying 
12 
this principle is the strong assumption in 
13 
capital market theory that companies earn the 
14 
same return on retained earnings as the market 
15 
demands on their common stock.   
16 
 
 
The DCF theory assures us that stocks only 
17 
have value because of the cash flows that 
18 
current investors receive or the anticipation of 
19 
cash flows that future investors hope to 
20 
receive.  Also fundamental to the DCF 
21 
methodology is the sentiment that cash and/or 
22 
earnings held in the future do not hold the same 
23 
worth as cash or earnings held in the present.  
24 
686


--- Page 687 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
62 
 
Due to the time preference of people to spend 
1 
their cash today rather than waiting for the 
2 
effects of inflation and productivity to impact 
3 
future cash flows, the DCF discounts the future 
4 
expected cash flows according to investors’ 
5 
return requirements. 
6 
Q. 
Why does the Panel place primary reliance on the 
7 
results of the DCF methodology? 
8 
A. 
The main reason the DCF methodology continues to 
9 
be the preferred approach for determining a 
10 
company’s cost of equity is that investors’ 
11 
immediate return requirements, as observed in 
12 
current stock prices and recent dividends, are 
13 
readily quantifiable.  The other principal 
14 
methodology, the CAPM, only relies tangentially, 
15 
through the use of utility beta values, upon 
16 
direct observations of actual utility investor 
17 
behavior.   
18 
 
 
The primary challenge in applying the DCF 
19 
is determining the rate of growth in future 
20 
dividends that investors expect.  However, given 
21 
the relatively mature and stable nature of the 
22 
utility industry, such estimates can be derived 
23 
with a reasonable degree of certitude.  Also, 
24 
687


--- Page 688 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
63 
 
rational utility investors expect the growth in 
1 
future dividends to generally track the changes 
2 
in output, or growth in the overall economy, as 
3 
measured by growth in the nominal Gross Domestic 
4 
Product, or GDP. 
5 
 
 
Moreover, just as nominal GDP growth 
6 
incorporates gains achieved through the 
7 
application of new technologies, otherwise known 
8 
as productivity, and the effects of changes in 
9 
price levels, the investors’ growth 
10 
expectations, too, will reflect assumptions 
11 
regarding productivity and the rate of 
12 
inflation.  Consequently, the intuitiveness of 
13 
the DCF methodology is abundantly clear with the 
14 
application of well-reasoned growth rate 
15 
estimates, such as those used in our approach.   
16 
 
 
This intuitiveness is a primary reason that 
17 
the Commission has regularly found this 
18 
methodology to be the best tool for estimating 
19 
the cost of equity for a regulated utility.  In 
20 
the Rate Order issued April 24, 2009, in the 
21 
Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. 
22 
Case 08-E-0539, the Commission stated that a 
23 
reason it accords a two-thirds weighting to the 
24 
688


--- Page 689 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
64 
 
DCF methodology is that “…the DCF relies on 
1 
readily available data to make objective 
2 
estimates of investors’ return requirements.  
3 
While the DCF has one input of primary 
4 
controversy (growth), two CAPM inputs (beta and 
5 
the market risk premium) are dependent on 
6 
estimates which are contested and volatile.”  
7 
Then, in the Rate Order for Corning’s last rate 
8 
case, 20-G-0101, issued on May 19, 2021, the 
9 
Commission once again affirmed Staff’s two-
10 
thirds DCF and one-third CAPM weighting of the 
11 
ROE.  In that Order, the Commission stated that 
12 
“Relying on more observable and less subjective 
13 
inputs, the DCF is superior to the CAPM and our 
14 
preferred weighting for determining an ultimate 
15 
ROE recognizes that superiority of the DCF.”     
16 
Q. 
Please describe the Panel’s DCF methodology and 
17 
its result. 
18 
A. 
Our DCF model is a two-stage “dividend discount” 
19 
model that is consistent with the financial 
20 
theory that the value of a company’s stock is 
21 
equivalent to its future cash flows.  Our 
22 
dividend discount model forecasts those cash 
23 
flows into the future and discounts them 
24 
689


--- Page 690 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
65 
 
 
back to their present value.  Our two-stage DCF 
1 
model is preferred, as it also explicitly 
2 
recognizes that a company’s short-term growth 
3 
expectations do not necessarily equal long-term 
4 
expectations.  The first stage uses analysts’ 
5 
near-term estimates to derive the short-term 
6 
growth rate, while the second stage is based on 
7 
a calculation of a sustainable growth rate.  Our 
8 
DCF calculation for the proxy group is shown on 
9 
pages 1 and 2 of Exhibit__(FP-6).

earnings per share, dividends per share, book

value per share, and forecasted amounts of

outstanding common stock for each company.

Our analysis maintains the same approach that

CAPITAL ASSET PRICING MODEL 
14 
Q. 
Please describe the basic theory underlying the 
15 
CAPM. 
16 
A. 
The principle behind the CAPM theory is that 
17 
there is no premium, in terms of expected 
18 
return, for bearing risks that can be eliminated 
19 
through diversification.  According to the CAPM, 
20 
rational investors will hold a portfolio of 
21 
stocks (generally 60 or more) such that the 
22 
overall risk of that portfolio, in terms of the 
23 
variability of its returns, closely approximates 
24 
696


--- Page 697 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
72 
 
that of the market as a whole.  Thus, the only 
1 
risk that matters in the CAPM equation is said 
2 
to be “systematic” risk, or risk that cannot be 
3 
diversified away.   
4 
Q.  Please explain systematic risk. 
5 
A. 
Systematic risk is a risk common to all equity 
6 
securities that cannot be eliminated through 
7 
diversification.  It is measured by a variable 
8 
denominated as “beta.”  Systematic risk is also 
9 
known as market risk, which is the uncertainty 
10 
inherent in the entire market or market segment.  
11 
Changes in interest rates, recessions, wars, and 
12 
pandemics are all examples of systematic risks. 
13 
Q.  What is unsystematic risk? 
14 
A. 
“Unsystematic” risk, on the other hand, is risk 
15 
that is specific to a particular stock.  While 
16 
it is assumed that most stocks tend to go along 
17 
with the general market, at least to some 
18 
extent, factors that are specific to an 
19 
individual stock are said to affect its 
20 
“unsystematic” risk. 
21 
Q.  How does the CAPM measure an individual stock’s 
22 
risk? 
23 
A. 
According to the CAPM, the appropriate way to 
24 
697


--- Page 698 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
73 
 
measure an individual stock’s risk is through a 
1 
correlation of its return relative to the market 
2 
as a whole, known as beta.  A stock with a beta 
3 
of 1.0 has a return that mirrors the return of 
4 
the “market,” usually taken to mean the S&P 500, 
5 
as a whole.  Betas of less than 1.0 indicate 
6 
that the stocks are less volatile than the 
7 
market as a whole.  Utility stocks, given the 
8 
moderating influence of regulation and the 
9 
accompanying perception of reduced risk, 
10 
typically have betas below 1.0.  Therefore, the 
11 
CAPM informs us that investors will only be 
12 
compensated for their actual risk, as measured 
13 
by beta.  In the case of estimating the return 
14 
requirements of utility investors, the CAPM 
15 
result will reflect the degree to which utility 
16 
stocks are less volatile than the market as a 
17 
whole. 
18 
Q. 
On what assumptions is the CAPM based? 
19 
A. 
The CAPM is based on the assumptions that: 1) 
20 
the capital market is competitive and efficient; 
21 
2) investors are risk-averse and demand higher 
22 
returns for higher risk; 3) market participants 
23 
can lend and borrow unlimited amounts under the 
24 
698


--- Page 699 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
74 
 
risk-free rate of interest; and 4) investors 
1 
hold diversified portfolios and operate in 
2 
capital markets with no transaction costs, 
3 
taxes, or restrictions on financial 
4 
transactions.  Under the CAPM, the expected 
5 
return of a security or a portfolio is equal to 
6 
the rate on a risk-free security plus a risk 
7 
premium multiplied by the asset’s systematic 
8 
risk.   
9 
Q. 
Please describe the methodology the Panel used 
10 
to determine its CAPM results. 
11 
A. 
Consistent with the approach that Staff has 
12 
employed and that the Commission has adopted for 
13 
many years, we averaged the results of two forms 
14 
of the CAPM: the Traditional CAPM and the Zero 
15 
Beta CAPM. 
16 
Q. 
Please describe the calculation used in the 
17 
Traditional CAPM. 
18 
A. 
The Traditional CAPM method calculates a 
19 
required return based on three inputs: the rate 
20 
of return on a risk-free rate investment (Rf), 
21 
the level of systematic risk for an investment 
22 
(β for beta), and the expected market risk 
23 
premium (MRP).  Typically, the MRP is calculated 
24 
699


--- Page 700 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
75 
 
by subtracting the risk-free rate from the 
1 
expected market return (Rm).  The form that the 
2 
Traditional CAPM takes is as follows: 
3 
 
 
Required Return (K) = Rf + β*(Rm-Rf). 
4 
Q.  Please describe the calculation used in the 
5 
Zero-Beta CAPM method. 
6 
A. 
We used the same inputs as in the Traditional 
7 
CAPM methodology; however, instead of 
8 
multiplying beta by the MRP, as shown in the 
9 
calculation of the Traditional CAPM methodology, 
10 
we determined the MRP for the proxy group by 
11 
multiplying 0.75 by beta by the MRP and adding 
12 
0.25 times the MRP.  This can be expressed as:   
13 
 
Required Return (K) = Rf + (0.75 * β * MRP) + 
14 
0.25 * (MRP). 
15 
Q. 
Why did the Panel use two forms of the CAPM? 
16 
A. 
We employ two CAPM methods because a 
17 
considerable body of research has indicated that 
18 
the Traditional CAPM model may underestimate the 
19 
required return when betas are below 1.0.  
20 
Therefore, to avoid an underestimated return, we 
21 
use a Zero Beta methodology as well.  By 
22 
averaging in the result of the Zero Beta 
23 
approach, which is only partially determined by 
24 
700


--- Page 701 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
76 
 
the beta used, this tendency is addressed and 
1 
corrected for, and ultimately enhances the 
2 
accuracy of our overall CAPM ROE determination.  
3

4

5 
A. 
The risk-free rate was estimated by averaging 
6

7

8 
September 2021.  The result for the three-month

11

13

We use the yields for two different Treasury

17

19

20

21

20

How did the Panel determine the appropriate beta 
22

23 
A. 
We used the 0.88 mean beta of our proxy group,

which we calculated using the most recent Value 
1

2 
proxy group. 
3 
Q. 
How does Value Line calculate beta? 
4 
A.  Value Line derives its beta from a regression 
5 
analysis of the relationship between weekly 
6 
percentage changes in the price of a stock and 
7 
weekly percentage changes in the New York Stock 
8 
Exchange Index over a period of five years.  
9 
Value Line also “smooths” the “coarse betas” to 
10 
reflect the theory that betas have a natural 
11 
tendency to converge to 1.0. 
12 
Q. 
Please explain how the calculation of beta can 
13 
be problematic. 
14 
A. 
First, beta is supposed to represent the future 
15 
volatility of a given stock relative to the 
16 
market as a whole.  However, because future 
17 
volatility is unknown, betas must be measured on 
18 
an historical basis.  The problem with using 
19 
historically derived betas, though, is that when 
20 
the systematic risks of a firm or industry 
21 
change, these historically derived betas may not 
22 
be reliable indicators of future volatility.  
23 
Thus, the measurement of past stock price 
24 
703


--- Page 704 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
79 
 
movements is a poor predictor of future stock 
1 
price changes.   
2 
 
 
A more significant shortcoming of beta 
3 
calculations is the often wide disparity in the 
4 
time frames firms use in their calculations.  
5 
For instance, Staff has exclusively relied on 
6 
betas reported by Value Line for at least the 
7 
past 25 years, as they are generally calculated 
8 
over a five-year period.  This is long enough to 
9 
produce reliable estimates but recent enough to 
10 
reflect current market conditions.  Some firms 
11 
use either much shorter or much longer time 
12 
periods in their calculations of beta.  We find 
13 
that the five-year time period used by Value 
14 
Line is sufficient in reducing volatility and 
15 
produces reliable estimates.  Moreover, Value 
16 
Line also “smoothes” the “raw” betas to reflect 
17 
the theory that betas have a natural tendency to 
18 
converge to 1.0.  Other firms do not adjust the 
19 
“raw” betas as Value Line does.  Our concern is 
20 
that, depending upon the source, betas can vary 
21 
significantly, and thus produce CAPM-based ROE 
22 
results that differ quite substantially solely 
23 
because of the source chosen for the beta input. 
24 
704


--- Page 705 ---
Case 21-G-0394

80 
 
Q.

1

3 
A. 
Because the cost of equity is, by its nature, a

11

averaged the required and implied market returns

of each of the three point-in-time forecasts, to

11.07%.  Excerpts of these publications are 
20 
included as Exhibit__(FP-14), and the full

24

returns in its calculation?

A.

14

15 
over time, there is no bias introduced as a

of data.

Q. 
How did the Panel determine the appropriate MRP 
19 
to use in its CAPM analysis? 
20 
A. 
As previously discussed, the MRP is the 
21 
difference between the expected market return on 
22 
the equity market and the return required on a 
23 
risk-free investment.  Subtracting our 1.63% 
24 
706


--- Page 707 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
82 
 
risk-free rate from the 11.07% cost of market 
1 
return yields our MRP estimate of 9.44%.  
2 
Q. 
Explain why the Panel did not rely on an ex-post 
3 
method to derive the appropriate MRP. 
4 
A. 
The application of an ex-post, or historical, 
5 
market risk premium method is problematic 
6 
because ex-post MRPs are based on the premise 
7 
that past performance is a valid proxy for 
8 
expectations regarding future results.  We 
9 
reject the underlying theory of this approach 
10 
because it has never been substantiated.  The 
11 
market risk premium is essentially a mean-
12 
reverting measure.  Furthermore, we are 
13 
disinclined to advocate such an approach because 
14 
it has been shown to periodically produce 
15 
counterintuitive results.  This approach has 
16 
also been known to be highly sensitive to the 
17 
actual time period selected to calculate the 
18 
premium.  From time to time, the actual market 
19 
return can become negative due to many factors, 
20 
including recessions, war, and/or depressed 
21 
earnings.  COVID-19 is an example of precisely 
22 
this kind of event risk.  Therefore, while 
23 
investors expect the market return to be 
24 
707


--- Page 708 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
83 
 
positive over the long run, they also expect the 
1 
market return to fluctuate in the short term, 
2 
punctuated by periods of negative return.  Due 
3 
to these structural shifts in the economy, the 
4 
application of an expected long-term market 
5 
return must consider realistic growth rates and 
6 
current economic factors. 
7 
Q. 
Has the Commission ever stated its preference 
8 
for relying on forward-looking (ex-ante) MRP 
9 
analyses as opposed to ex-post analyses? 
10 
A.

this market risk premium methodology since the

18 
calculation based on Merrill Lynch data is a 
19 
reasonable method of deriving a risk premium; 
20 
and it avoids the problem of stale data in the

16 
A. 
Concentric calculated six multi-stage DCF 
17 
calculations to inform its ROE recommendation 
18 
range.  The DCF calculations are based on an 
19 
analysis of the two proxy groups of utility 
20 
holding companies.  For both of the proxy 
21 
groups, Concentric calculated three DCF 
22 
estimates using the low, mean, and high

estimated earnings growth rates from three 
24 
729


--- Page 730 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
105 
 
sources (Value Line, Yahoo! Finance, and 
1 
Zack’s), yielding six DCF calculations. 
2 
Q. 
Please briefly describe the three stages of 
3 
Concentric’s multi-stage DCF models. 
4 
A. 
The first stage of Concentric’s multi-stage DCF 
5 
model is calculated using short-term earnings 
6 
per share growth rate estimates from Value Line, 
7 
Yahoo! Finance, and Zacks.  These published 
8 
forecasts inform three different growth rate 
9 
scenarios.  One scenario is based on the highest 
10 
of these forecasts, another is based on the 
11 
lowest, and a third is based on the mean of 
12 
these estimates.   
13 
 
 
Concentric’s second stage is effectively a 
14 
blend of its first and third stage growth rates, 
15 
whereby each company’s imputed short-term 
16 
earnings growth rates gradually converge towards 
17 
Concentric’s forecasted long-term GDP growth 
18 
rates.  Concentric’s third stage uses a long-
19 
term GDP growth rate that is derived from 
20 
forecasted inflation rates and historic economic 
21 
growth rates. 
22

23

A. 
We are concerned about Concentric’s application 
1 
of: 1) earnings growth rates rather than 
2

3

5 
Q. 
Please explain why Concentric’s use of earnings 
6 
rather than dividends to estimate the short-term 
7 
growth rates in its DCF model is problematic. 
8 
A. 
Concentric’s DCF model uses earnings growth rate 
9 
forecasts published by analysts in order to 
10 
estimate short-term growth in dividends.  This 
11 
approach assumes that growth in dividends will 
12 
approximate growth in earnings, although 
13 
Concentric did not provide any evidence 
14 
demonstrating that this assumption is valid.  
15 
Concentric’s assumption is unproven and 
16 
unnecessary, given that dividend growth rates or 
17 
forecasts are readily available.  This approach 
18 
also stands in direct contrast to the basic 
19 
premise of the DCF, which measures the present 
20 
value of future dividends, not earnings. 
21 
Q.  How can Concentric’s use of earnings growth 
22 
instead of dividend growth lead to inaccuracy in 
23 
its DCF model? 
24 
731


--- Page 732 ---
Case 21-G-0394  
 
FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
107 
 
A.  Concentric's use of earnings growth in its DCF 
1 
model fails to properly account for the division 
2 
of annual earnings into retained earnings and 
3 
dividends.  Investors recognize that annual 
4 
earnings represent a company's profit before the 
5 
consideration of its dividend payout and the use 
6 
of retained earnings.  Retained earnings provide 
7 
a company’s management with the flexibility to 
8 
maintain its current dividends should it suffer 
9 
a loss of revenue or unplanned expenses, 
10 
effectively providing a cushion for investors 
11 
when profitability shrinks.  In fact, a 
12 
company’s dividend policy is one of the ways 
13 
that it insulates shareholders from the 
14 
volatility of earnings from one time period to 
15 
the next.  Indeed, investors generally prefer 
16 
dividends to be steadily increasing and 
17 
predictably regular.  Thus, Concentric's primary 
18 
reliance on earnings growth in its DCF model 
19 
rather than dividend growth reflects neither 
20 
realistic growth rates nor typical corporate 
21 
practice. 
22 
Q. 
What additional reasons make Concentric’s 
23 
application of earnings growth, rather than 
24 
732

FINANCE PANEL

dividend growth, in its DCF model problematic?

Our DCF model is more comprehensive because it

reflected in the stock price.  Corporations
